components.name: End User (Browser)
components.description: Employee or attacker using a browser to reach the RetireEasy/NodeGoat web application over HTTP on port 4000. Submits login, signup, profile, contributions, benefits, memos and research forms.
assets: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers

components.name: NodeGoat Express Application
components.description: Node.js/Express server (server.js) that mounts body-parser, express-session and Swig/consolidate templating, connects to MongoDB and registers all application routes in app/routes/index.js. Helmet, csurf and dont-sniff-mimetype are present as dependencies but their use is commented out in server.js.

components.name: Session/Auth Handler
components.description: SessionHandler implements login, signup, logout and the isLoggedInMiddleware / isAdminUserMiddleware guards based on req.session.userId. Login passwords are compared against stored values with === via UserDAO.validateLogin.

components.name: Profile Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /profile: reads firstName, lastName, ssn, dob, address, bankAcc and bankRouting from the request body, validates bankRouting with a nested-quantifier regex, and persists via ProfileDAO.updateUser.

components.name: Contributions Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /contributions. Parses preTax, afterTax and roth request body values with eval() before range checks, then stores them through ContributionsDAO.

components.name: Allocations Handler
components.description: Handles GET /allocations/:userId, taking the userId from the URL parameter rather than the session and passing a threshold query value into AllocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, which interpolates it into a MongoDB $where clause.

components.name: Benefits Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /benefits, listing all non-admin users and updating any user's benefitStartDate by userId taken from the request body. Renders with user.isAdmin hard-coded true and is registered with only isLoggedIn, not isAdmin.

components.name: Memos Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /memos: inserts req.body.memo into the memos collection and renders all memos, which are passed through marked() in the template.
assets: memo content shared between all users

components.name: Research Handler
components.description: Handles GET /research. When a symbol query parameter is present it concatenates req.query.url with req.query.symbol and fetches that URL with needle, writing the remote response body directly into the HTTP response.
assets: outbound request capability from the server network position

components.name: Learn Redirect Endpoint
components.description: GET /learn handler defined inline in app/routes/index.js that redirects the browser to whatever URL is supplied in the url query string parameter, with no allow-list.

components.name: Tutorial Router
components.description: Unauthenticated Express router mounted at /tutorial that renders static Swig tutorial pages (a1..a10, redos, ssrf) describing the intentional vulnerabilities.

components.name: Swig Template Views
components.description: Server-rendered HTML views (layout, dashboard, profile, memos, benefits, allocations, error-template) rendered by Swig via consolidate. The memos view calls marked() on stored memo content and the error template prints the raw error object.

components.name: Error Handling Middleware
components.description: Express error middleware that logs err.message and err.stack to the console and renders error-template with the error object, returning HTTP 500.
assets: internal error details and stack traces

components.name: MongoDB (nodegoat)
components.description: MongoDB 4.4 instance holding the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections. Reached via the mongodb 2.x driver using the connection string in MONGODB_URI (defaults to mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat, mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat in docker-compose).

components.name: Database Reset Seeder
components.description: artifacts/db-reset.js script run at container start and via npm run db:seed; it drops collections and inserts fixed admin/user1/user2 accounts with hard-coded passwords.

components.name: External Stock Quote Site
components.description: Third-party HTTP endpoint fetched server-side by the research handler; the form defaults to https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/ but the host is taken from the request, so any attacker-chosen host can be contacted.

components.name: OWASP ZAP Proxy (security tests)
components.description: ZAP instance configured by host, port and API key in the development and test config files and driven by test/security/profile-test.js through the zaproxy client.

components.name: GitHub Actions CI
components.description: CI workflows that check out the repository, install dependencies, start MongoDB in Docker and run Cypress end-to-end tests and jshint linting.

components.name: mongodb datastore
components.description: Datastore detected from mongodb in package.json.

components.name: web (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) web defined in docker-compose.yml, ports 4000.

components.name: e2e-test.yml:e2e-test (github_actions)
components.description: Deployment target (github_actions) e2e-test.yml:e2e-test defined in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.

components.name: lint.yml:lint (github_actions)
components.description: Deployment target (github_actions) lint.yml:lint defined in .github/workflows/lint.yml.

trustBoundaries.name: Public internet to Express application
trustBoundaries.description: Browser traffic arrives over plain HTTP on port 4000 (HTTPS setup is commented out in server.js) and reaches Express route handlers. Unauthenticated routes (/, /login, /signup, /logout, /tutorial) sit on the outside; session-guarded routes sit on the inside.

trustBoundaries.name: Unauthenticated to authenticated session
trustBoundaries.description: isLoggedInMiddleware promotes a request from anonymous to a logged-in user based on req.session.userId, granting access to dashboard, profile, contributions, allocations, memos, learn and research.

trustBoundaries.name: Regular user to administrative benefits function
trustBoundaries.description: The benefits module is an administrative function (isAdminUserMiddleware exists in session.js) but its routes are registered with only isLoggedIn, so a normal user crosses into admin-level data without a role check.

trustBoundaries.name: Application process to MongoDB
trustBoundaries.description: All DAOs talk to a separate MongoDB 4.4 service over the MongoDB wire protocol using the MONGODB_URI connection string; the $where interpolation in allocations-dao.js lets request data become server-side JavaScript executed by the database.

trustBoundaries.name: Application to third-party HTTP services
trustBoundaries.description: The research handler makes outbound needle.get requests to a host taken from the request, and the security test harness proxies through an external ZAP instance.

trustBoundaries.name: CI pipeline to running application
trustBoundaries.description: GitHub Actions checks out the repository, boots the app with NODE_ENV=test and a disposable MongoDB container, and exercises it with Cypress.

unknowns.description: Input validation for GET /learn on NodeGoat Express Application, Learn Redirect Endpoint could not be confirmed; it may be supplied by middleware, configuration or infrastructure this analysis cannot follow (detector certainty 0.55).

Does the NodeGoat Express Application record security-relevant events (failed logins, benefit changes, profile updates) anywhere other than console.log in Error Handling Middleware and the DAOs, so that abuse of Benefits Handler or Allocations Handler could be detected?

Is outbound access from the Research Handler to External Stock Quote Site restricted to an allow-list of hosts at the network level, so the server cannot be made to reach internal addresses or cloud metadata endpoints?
Does the Error Handling Middleware suppress the raw error object in production instead of rendering it into error-template.html, so internal stack details are not returned to End User (Browser)?

Is memo content rendered by Swig Template Views through marked() in the Memos Handler sanitized or HTML-escaped before display, so that one user's stored memo cannot execute script in another user's browser?

Does the MongoDB (nodegoat) instance require authentication with a least-privilege user for the NodeGoat Express Application, rather than the credential-less mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat URI used in docker-compose.yml?
Is the data stored by MongoDB (nodegoat) — including plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank account numbers written by Profile Handler — encrypted at rest?
Is any rate limiting or account lockout applied to the POST /login and POST /signup endpoints in the Session/Auth Handler, so that the plaintext-compared passwords cannot be brute forced?

Is the Database Reset Seeder (artifacts/db-reset.js, run from docker-compose and app.json postdeploy) prevented from running against a production MongoDB (nodegoat), given that it recreates the well-known admin account?

Are the express-session cookies issued by the Session/Auth Handler configured with httpOnly, secure and an explicit expiry/maxAge, so that a stolen or long-lived session cannot be replayed against the NodeGoat Express Application?

Is traffic between End User (Browser) and the NodeGoat Express Application terminated over TLS by a proxy in production, given that the HTTPS setup in server.js is commented out and Dockerfile/docker-compose expose plain HTTP on port 4000, which would otherwise expose session cookies and SSN/bank data in transit?

Are the ZAP API key and host values in config/env/development.js and config/env/test.js used only against a local OWASP ZAP Proxy (security tests) instance and never shipped in the deployed NodeGoat Express Application image?

threats.title: MongoDB wire traffic between the application and mongo is unauthenticated and unencrypted
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details in transit on the MongoDB connection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used by MongoClient.connect in server.js:30 is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat from docker-compose.yml:8, with no credentials and no TLS options, so anyone who can reach the mongo service on the Docker network reads or rewrites allocations and users documents on the wire, or connects directly as an unauthenticated client and dumps the collection.
assumptions: An attacker can obtain a foothold on the container network or the host.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The mongo container is started without --auth and without TLS, as the compose file supplies no credentials or certificate configuration.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated wire access exposes and allows modification of every collection, including plaintext passwords and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network access to the container network rather than a plain internet request. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Create a least-privilege MongoDB user and put its credentials in MONGODB_URI via a secret rather than the literal in docker-compose.yml:8.
Start the mongo service with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS and add tls=true to the URI consumed in config/env/all.js:3.

threats.title: Session cookie for the allocations session travels in cleartext over HTTP
threats.asset: authenticated session cookie granting access to /allocations/:userId
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the express-session cookie at server.js:78 is configured without secure, so an attacker on the same network as a victim captures the session cookie from the plaintext GET /allocations/:userId request and replays it to read the victim's allocations as them.
assumptions: The application is reachable over plain HTTP in deployment with no TLS-terminating proxy in front of it, as docker-compose.yml publishes port 4000 directly.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full authenticated access to the victim's account and its financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position between the victim and the server, but the transport is unencrypted by default.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 and drop the plain http listener.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Cookie-session requests to the allocations handler carry no CSRF token
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated NodeGoat session and the actions reachable with it
threats.attackScenario: csurf is commented out in server.js:104-113 and the session cookie is sent on cross-site requests with no SameSite restriction, so an attacker's page issues a forged request to a state-changing NodeGoat route while the victim is logged in from the allocations page, with the browser attaching the session cookie automatically and the server accepting it without a token.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site requests because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: Forged authenticated requests can change the victim's profile, contributions or benefits data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the victim to visit an attacker page while logged in, but no token barrier exists.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens for all cookie-authenticated state-changing routes.
steps: Uncomment the csurf setup at server.js:104-113 and add the csrftoken hidden field to the forms in app/views.
Set cookie: { sameSite: 'lax' } in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let a hostile page frame and drive the allocations view
threats.asset: the victim's rendered allocations page and their authenticated session
threats.attackScenario: helmet is commented out in server.js and no frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy is set, so an attacker hosts a page that iframes /allocations/<victimId> and overlays decoy controls to clickjack a logged-in victim into interacting with the allocations UI, while the absent CSP means any injected markup in the swig template (autoescape is disabled at server.js:137) runs unrestricted in the victim's session.
assumptions: The deployment does not add security headers at a reverse proxy in front of Express.
threats.impactReason: Framing and the absence of a script policy remove the browser-side containment around an authenticated financial view.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any attacker-controlled page can frame the route; only a logged-in victim visiting it is needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet with frameguard, CSP and nosniff.
steps: Uncomment and update the helmet block at server.js:38-65, using current helmet APIs for frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy and hsts.
Re-enable swig autoescape at server.js:135-142.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through the threshold parameter on GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: all documents in the nodegoat MongoDB database, including plaintext user passwords and SSN/bank details
threats.attackScenario: AllocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold interpolates the raw threshold query value into a $where JavaScript string at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, so an attacker requests GET /allocations/1?threshold=1'; return this.userId == this.userId || '1 to break out of the quoted comparison and have the mongod server evaluate attacker JavaScript over every document, returning allocations for all users and enabling boolean-oracle extraction of fields such as password from the users collection.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary JavaScript executed inside the database engine exposes and can iterate over every collection, including plaintext passwords stored by user-dao.js.
threats.likelihoodReason: The threshold field is a plain text input on the allocations page and the injection needs only a crafted query string on an authenticated session.

mitigation.summary: Remove the $where clause and filter with typed query operators.
steps: Replace the interpolated $where at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77-79 with {userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}}.
Parse threshold with parseInt(threshold, 10) and reject values outside 0-99 before querying, as the commented-out block at lines 70-75 shows.
Restore the numeric input constraint in app/views/allocations.html:22 for UX defence in depth.

threats.title: No audit trail for cross-user allocation access, so enumeration is repudiable
threats.asset: audit record of who read which user's allocation data
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId serves any requested user id with no ownership check and the handler at app/routes/allocations.js:23 records nothing about who asked for which id, so an attacker who walks /allocations/1..N to harvest other users' allocations leaves no server-side record tying the reads to their session, and can deny having performed them.
assumptions: Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
No reverse proxy or external access log correlating session identity to requested userId is deployed in front of the Express server.
threats.impactReason: Without per-request identity logging, mass scraping of allocation records cannot be attributed or scoped during an investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every request to the route goes unlogged by default, so the condition holds for any attacker who reaches it. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Log authenticated identity alongside the requested resource id for allocation reads.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js:23, emit a log entry containing req.session.userId, req.params.userId and the request timestamp before calling the DAO.
Flag and alert when req.session.userId differs from req.params.userId.

threats.title: Any authenticated user reads another user's allocations by changing the :userId path segment
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records and real names
threats.attackScenario: displayAllocations takes userId from req.params at app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 instead of req.session, and no ownership or role check guards GET /allocations/:userId, so an attacker logs in with any account and requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to enumerate every user's stocks, funds and bonds together with their first and last names.
assumptions: User ids are small sequential integers, as parseInt(userId) in allocations-dao.js implies.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation breakdown and name is readable one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account reaches the route and the ids are sequential integers.

mitigation.summary: Derive the user id from the session rather than the URL.
steps: Replace `const { userId } = req.params;` at app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 with `const { userId } = req.session;` as the commented fix at lines 13-15 indicates.
If an admin view of other users is needed, gate it on an explicit isAdmin check in the route middleware in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Injected $where JavaScript pivots the Allocations-to-MongoDB flow into reading other collections
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank account details stored in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The find() sent over the MongoDB wire protocol on this flow carries an attacker-controlled JavaScript predicate built at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, so an attacker submits boolean payloads in threshold such as 1' || this.userId==1 && /^a/.test(this.password) || ' and observes which allocation rows come back, extracting the plaintext passwords that user-dao.js stores unhashed one character at a time.
assumptions: The allocations and users documents are in the same database that the $where predicate can reference through the evaluated scope or through repeated boolean probes.
threats.impactReason: Plaintext credentials and bank details leak through an ordinary-looking allocations response.
threats.likelihoodReason: The oracle is directly observable in the rendered page and needs only repeated query-string requests.

mitigation.summary: Eliminate JavaScript evaluation on the query path to MongoDB.
steps: Use {stocks: {$gt: Number(threshold)}} at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 instead of $where.
Run mongod with --noscripting in docker-compose.yml.
Hash passwords with bcrypt in app/data/user-dao.js:25 so a database-side oracle yields no usable secret.

threats.title: Denial of service by injecting an infinite loop into the MongoDB $where evaluation
threats.asset: availability of the MongoDB instance and the allocations service
threats.attackScenario: Because the threshold value is interpolated into the $where JavaScript at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, an attacker sends GET /allocations/1?threshold=0';while(true){}' so that mongod spins in a never-ending loop evaluating the clause, pinning a database thread and starving all other NodeGoat queries.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment allows server-side JavaScript execution (javascriptEnabled) and does not impose an operation timeout on $where evaluation.
threats.impactReason: A single request can hang the shared database process, taking down every feature of the application until the operation is killed.
threats.likelihoodReason: The payload is a one-line query string and the exploit is documented in a comment in the same file.

mitigation.summary: Stop passing user input into server-side JavaScript and bound query execution.
steps: Switch the query at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 to the $gt operator so no JavaScript is evaluated.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --noscripting.
Set maxTimeMS on the find() call in app/data/allocations-dao.js:86.

threats.title: Long-running injected predicates on the allocations query exhaust the shared MongoDB connection
threats.asset: availability of the MongoDB connection shared by every NodeGoat DAO
threats.attackScenario: The find() at app/data/allocations-dao.js:86 is issued on the single MongoClient connection created in server.js:30 with no maxTimeMS, so an attacker repeatedly calls GET /allocations/1?threshold=0';while(true){}' to queue expensive $where evaluations on that one connection and block queries from user-dao, profile-dao and benefits-dao as well.
assumptions: A single shared MongoClient connection serves all DAOs and no server-side operation timeout is configured.
threats.impactReason: Saturating the shared database connection makes login and every other data-backed page unavailable.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivially repeatable requests, though it needs an authenticated session and sustained traffic.

mitigation.summary: Bound query cost and remove the JavaScript predicate.
steps: Add maxTimeMS to the find() call at app/data/allocations-dao.js:86.
Replace the $where clause with the $gt operator so evaluation cost is bounded by the index.
Configure a connection pool size and timeouts in the MongoClient.connect options in server.js:30.

threats.title: Login error messages distinguish unknown username from wrong password
threats.asset: valid NodeGoat usernames
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:58-89 renders 'Invalid username' when userDAO.validateLogin reports noSuchUser and a different password message otherwise, so an attacker POSTs a list of candidate userNames to /login with a junk password and keeps every name that does not return 'Invalid username' as a confirmed account for password guessing.
assumptions: Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
No rate limiting or account lockout sits in front of POST /login in the deployment.
threats.impactReason: Enumerated usernames are a precursor to credential stuffing rather than a direct data loss.
threats.likelihoodReason: POST /login is unauthenticated and the distinguishing responses are returned on every attempt. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Return one generic authentication failure message for both cases.
steps: Use the existing `errorMessage` constant ('Invalid username and/or password') for both the noSuchUser and invalidPassword branches in app/routes/session.js.
Add per-IP and per-account throttling in front of app.post("/login") in app/routes/index.js:34.

threats.title: No CSRF protection on POST /login, /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos
threats.asset: user profile data and benefits/contributions records
threats.attackScenario: app.use(csrf()) is commented out at server.js:104-113 and no token is checked at app/routes/index.js:34, so an attacker hosts a page with a hidden form auto-submitting to https://nodegoat-host/profile and any logged-in victim who visits it has their profile fields (including bank account details) overwritten with attacker values.
assumptions: Browsers send the session cookie on the cross-site POST because no SameSite attribute is configured on it.
threats.impactReason: Cross-site forged posts rewrite profile, contribution and benefit records for any victim, and login CSRF can pin a victim into an attacker-controlled account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user visiting an attacker page triggers it, though modern browser SameSite=Lax defaults blunt some cross-site POSTs.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already listed as a dependency and emit tokens in forms.
steps: Uncomment `app.use(csrf())` and the res.locals.csrftoken middleware at server.js:104-113.
Add the hidden csrftoken input to every POST form template (login, signup, profile, contributions, benefits, memos).
Set `sameSite: "strict"` on the session cookie in server.js:78 as defence in depth.

threats.title: Passwords stored and compared in cleartext by the login/signup flow
threats.asset: user account passwords
threats.attackScenario: UserDAO.addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:25 writes the raw password field into the MongoDB users collection and validateLogin at app/data/user-dao.js:60-61 compares it with a plain === , so anyone who reaches the nodegoat database (for example through the docker-compose mongo service at docker-compose.yml:13-17 with no credentials configured) dumps every user's usable password and logs in as them over POST /login.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The deployed MongoDB instance holds real user records created through the signup route.
threats.impactReason: Every account password is directly readable and reusable, including on other sites where users reuse passwords.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires read access to the database or a backup, but the bcrypt hashing code is commented out so no additional weakness is needed once reached. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with the bcrypt-nodejs dependency already present.
steps: Uncomment and use `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` in this.addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:25.
Replace the `fromDB === fromUser` comparison in validateLogin with bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB) at app/data/user-dao.js:60.
Migrate existing cleartext passwords by re-hashing on next successful login and clearing the plain value.

threats.title: Credential and session data on the app-to-session dispatch path is neither CSRF-bound nor protected by response headers
threats.asset: user credentials and session identifiers carried to SessionHandler
threats.attackScenario: The dispatch from app/routes/index.js:34 into sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest carries the POSTed userName and password with no CSRF token check and no framing or CSP headers on the responses, so an attacker frames the NodeGoat login page or auto-submits a cross-site form of their own credentials and causes the victim's browser to establish a session bound to the attacker's account before the victim enters data into it.
assumptions: The login page is renderable inside a third-party frame because no X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors directive is emitted.
threats.impactReason: Login CSRF and clickjacking on this path let an attacker capture data the victim subsequently enters under an attacker-controlled session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Both the csurf middleware and every helmet header are commented out in server.js, and the login route is unauthenticated.

mitigation.summary: Enable csurf and helmet on the routes that dispatch into SessionHandler.
steps: Uncomment app.use(csrf()) at server.js:107 so POST /login and POST /signup require a token.
Uncomment helmet.frameguard(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.hsts(), nosniff() and app.disable("x-powered-by") at server.js:38-65.

threats.title: Session fixation: express-session saves uninitialised sessions and never regenerates the id at login
threats.asset: session identifiers and the authenticated sessions they represent
threats.attackScenario: server.js:84-85 sets saveUninitialized true and resave true while handleLoginRequest in app/routes/session.js only sets req.session.userId without calling req.session.regenerate, so an attacker fetches / to obtain a connect.sid, plants it in a victim's browser via a crafted link and then reuses that same id once the victim logs in to ride their authenticated session.
assumptions: The login handler assigns req.session.userId on the existing session rather than regenerating it.
threats.impactReason: A fixed session id yields full account takeover including profile and allocation data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anonymous sessions are issued to any visitor of GET /, but the attacker still needs a way to plant the cookie in the victim's browser.

mitigation.summary: Regenerate the session id on successful authentication and stop persisting anonymous sessions.
steps: Call req.session.regenerate() before setting req.session.userId in handleLoginRequest in app/routes/session.js.
Set saveUninitialized: false and resave: false in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Set an explicit generic cookie key and maxAge as shown in the commented block at server.js:86-100.

threats.title: Login attempts logged without repudiation-resistant records or CRLF encoding
threats.asset: authentication audit trail
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/session.js:64 writes the raw userName into console.log for failed logins with the ESAPI encoding left commented out at lines 66-80, so an attacker submits a userName containing \r\n plus a fabricated 'Connected to the database' line and forges log entries that hide their own brute-force attempts against POST /login.
assumptions: Application stdout is the record used to investigate authentication incidents.
Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
threats.impactReason: Forged or polluted log lines undermine attribution of failed and successful logins but do not directly expose data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The userName is attacker-controlled on every unauthenticated POST /login and reaches console.log unencoded. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Encode user input before logging and record successful as well as failed authentications.
steps: Use the node-esapi dependency already in package.json to encode userName before console.log in app/routes/session.js:64, or strip /(\r\n|\r|\n)/g.
Emit structured log records including outcome, source IP and timestamp for both successful and failed logins, and ship them off-host.

threats.title: Rendered pages carry no security headers, so an injected or framed view runs without CSP or clickjacking protection
threats.asset: user profile data rendered in Swig templates
threats.attackScenario: Responses produced by res.render of app/views/layout.html carry no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options because the helmet middleware is commented out, so an attacker frames /profile on their own page and overlays invisible buttons to make a logged-in victim submit the /profile form with attacker-chosen bank account values, and any injected script in a template has no CSP to block its outbound requests.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds security response headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Clickjacked form submissions can alter profile and benefits records, and the absence of CSP removes the last barrier against injected script in the unescaped templates.
threats.likelihoodReason: Framing requires only that a victim visit an attacker page while logged in; no privileged position is needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet, which is already a declared dependency, before the routes are mounted.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and add app.use(helmet()) before routes(app, db) at server.js:132.
Configure a Content-Security-Policy that disallows inline script, and keep frameguard and noSniff enabled.
Call app.disable("x-powered-by").

threats.title: Swig autoescape disabled lets stored profile and memo data render as executable HTML in the app's views
threats.asset: rendered user profile and allocation data shown to other logged-in users
threats.attackScenario: server.js:135-142 calls swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }), so an attacker saves <script>fetch('/profile',{method:'POST',body:'bankAcc=...'})</script> into the lastName field posted to /profile and the payload is emitted raw by {{lastName}} in app/views/profile.html:45 and by {{allocation.firstName}} in app/views/allocations.html:35, executing in a victim's logged-in session and silently changing their profile or reading /allocations pages on their behalf.
assumptions: The profile and allocation fields rendered in these templates are not individually escaped before res.render is called.
threats.impactReason: Script running in a victim session can read and submit to /profile, /benefits and /allocations, reaching SSN, date of birth and bank account numbers; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly so it is not readable by the script.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can store a payload through the /profile form and the rendering path is unescaped by configuration.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable Swig autoescaping and escape any value that must contain markup explicitly.
steps: Change swig.setDefaults at server.js:135 to autoescape: true.
Where raw HTML is genuinely required (memo markdown), keep marked's sanitize option and use node-esapi, already a dependency, to encode the remaining fields.
Remove the raw {{lastName}}, {{ssn}}, {{bankAcc}} usages in app/views/profile.html in favour of the escaped SafeString pattern already used for firstNameSafeString.

threats.title: Error template echoes raw error output to the browser
threats.asset: stack-trace and internal error output
threats.attackScenario: The error view app/views/error-template.html:11 prints {{error}} directly into the response body, and with Swig autoescape disabled at server.js:137 an attacker triggers a failure — for example by sending a malformed threshold to /allocations/:userId — and reads MongoDB driver messages, file paths and stack frames returned in the rendered Internal Error page.
assumptions: The error handler passes the full error object, rather than a generic message, into the error-template render in production.
threats.impactReason: Internal paths, driver versions and query structure help an attacker build follow-on NoSQL injection against the allocations collection.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can provoke a handler error with malformed query input; no special tooling is needed.

mitigation.summary: Render a generic message to users and log the detail server-side only.
steps: In app/routes/error.js, log the error object and pass only a static message string into res.render for app/views/error-template.html.
Escape {{error}} in app/views/error-template.html once autoescaping is re-enabled.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery changes any employee's benefit start date via POST /benefits
threats.asset: all employees' benefit start dates
threats.attackScenario: POST /benefits accepts a plain form body (app/views/benefits.html posts userId and benefitStartDate) and no CSRF token is validated, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to http://<app>/benefits with userId=1&benefitStartDate=2099-01-01 and any logged-in employee who visits it silently rewrites that user's benefits record using their session cookie.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates for arbitrary users can be altered without the victim's knowledge.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user visiting an attacker-controlled page triggers the write; no token blocks it.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation for state-changing routes.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware already referenced in server.js:7 and server.js:107 and expose res.locals.csrftoken.
Add the hidden _csrf input to the form in app/views/benefits.html.
Set cookie SameSite=Lax on the express-session cookie in server.js:78.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB wire traffic carrying the users collection can be read or rewritten on the container network
threats.asset: users collection contents including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details
threats.attackScenario: The connection string in config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials and no TLS parameters, so anyone who reaches the mongo service on the compose network connects as an anonymous client, reads the users collection that benefits-to-mongo queries, and issues their own $set updates against benefitStartDate or password fields.
assumptions: An attacker can obtain a foothold on the same Docker network or host as the mongo container.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
MongoDB is started without authentication enabled and without TLS, as the credential-free URI in docker-compose.yml:8 implies.
threats.impactReason: The users collection holds plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details for every employee and can be both read and rewritten.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to the mongo container, but once there no authentication or transport encryption stands in the way. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Start the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and a dedicated application user restricted to the nodegoat database.
Supply MONGODB_URI with credentials and tls=true from a secret rather than the literal in config/env/all.js:3.
Restrict the mongo container so only the web service can reach port 27017.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee can read the full employee roster and edit any user's benefit start date via /benefits
threats.asset: all employees' benefit start dates and the employee roster
threats.attackScenario: GET /benefits (app/routes/index.js:55) and POST /benefits (app/routes/index.js:56) are registered with only isLoggedIn, and app/routes/benefits.js renders with a hard-coded user.isAdmin=true, so a self-registered employee browses to /benefits, sees every non-admin user's id, first name, last name and benefit start date, then POSTs userId=<someone else's id>&benefitStartDate=2099-01-01 to rewrite another employee's benefits record.
assumptions: The isAdmin middleware is not applied elsewhere in front of the /benefits routes.
threats.impactReason: The whole non-admin employee roster is disclosed and any employee's benefit start date can be silently altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a normal application account is required; the admin-only UI is served to every authenticated caller.

mitigation.summary: Enforce an admin role check on the /benefits routes and stop hard-coding isAdmin in the view model.
steps: Register GET/POST /benefits in app/routes/index.js with the existing isAdmin middleware in addition to isLoggedIn.
In app/routes/benefits.js replace `user: { isAdmin: true }` with the session user object so the template reflects the real role.
Validate that req.body.userId refers to a user the caller is permitted to administer before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.

threats.title: Missing security response headers allow the benefits admin page to be framed and its markup abused
threats.asset: all employees' benefit start dates
threats.attackScenario: No helmet or header configuration is applied, so an attacker frames /benefits on a lookalike page, overlays a decoy button over the Save control in app/views/benefits.html, and a logged-in employee's click submits the hidden userId/benefitStartDate form, altering another user's benefits record; the absent Content-Security-Policy also leaves the swig-rendered roster page with no script-source restriction.
assumptions: The application is served without a reverse proxy that injects X-Frame-Options or CSP headers.
threats.impactReason: Clickjacked writes change benefits data and the missing CSP removes a defence against injected script running in the admin page.
threats.likelihoodReason: Framing needs only a victim who is logged in and visits the attacker's page.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet with frameguard and a content security policy.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and register helmet() before routes(app, db) at server.js:132.
Configure frameguard deny, nosniff and a script-src 'self' content security policy.

threats.title: Unauthenticated NoSQL operator injection into the benefits update filter
threats.asset: all employees' benefit start dates in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: POST /benefits takes userId and benefitStartDate straight from req.body (app/routes/benefits.js:29-35) with no type or value validation and passes benefitStartDate unvalidated into the Mongo `$set` in app/data/benefits-dao.js:23-30, so a logged-in user submits a JSON body such as {"userId":"1","benefitStartDate":{"a":1}} and writes an arbitrary attacker-chosen document value into the users collection, corrupting the benefits record.
assumptions: bodyParser.json() allows non-string JSON values to reach req.body for this route, so benefitStartDate need not be a string.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary values can be written into user documents, corrupting benefits data used by downstream handlers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can post JSON directly; no validation stands between the body and the update.

mitigation.summary: Validate and coerce userId and benefitStartDate before building the Mongo update.
steps: In app/routes/benefits.js reject the request unless benefitStartDate is a string matching an ISO date pattern and userId parses to a positive integer.
In app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 coerce startDate with String(startDate) and guard against NaN from parseInt(userId).

threats.title: Benefit changes are written with no attributable audit record
threats.asset: audit trail of benefit start date changes
threats.attackScenario: updateBenefits in app/data/benefits-dao.js only prints the literal string "Updated benefits" with no actor, target userId or previous value, so an employee who changes a colleague's benefitStartDate through POST /benefits leaves no record identifying who made the change and later denies it.
assumptions: Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
No external audit logging wraps the benefits routes.
threats.impactReason: HR-relevant data changes cannot be attributed or rolled back during investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every use of the update path is unlogged, so the gap is exercised by any change. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Emit an attributable audit event for every benefits update.
steps: In app/routes/benefits.js log the session user id, target userId, old and new benefitStartDate on each successful update.
Ship these records to an append-only log store outside the application process.

threats.title: Unbounded roster query on every /benefits request exhausts the application and database
threats.asset: availability of the benefits listing and the MongoDB instance
threats.attackScenario: getAllNonAdminUsers in app/data/benefits-dao.js:15-20 runs an unpaginated find({isAdmin:{$ne:true}}).toArray() that is executed once for GET /benefits and a second time after every POST /benefits update, so a logged-in user loops POST /benefits requests and forces repeated full-collection scans that load the entire users collection into memory and saturate the Mongo connection.
assumptions: No rate limiting is applied in front of the /benefits routes.
The users collection grows large enough that full scans are expensive.
threats.impactReason: Repeated full-collection reads degrade or stall the single Express process and the shared Mongo instance for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated account can script the POST loop; no throttle or pagination limits the work.

mitigation.summary: Paginate the roster query and rate-limit the benefits routes.
steps: Add skip/limit and a projection to the find() in app/data/benefits-dao.js:16 so only a page of users is materialised.
Apply a request rate limiter to POST /benefits in app/routes/index.js.
Index isAdmin so the filter does not require a collection scan.

threats.title: Missing CSRF protection lets an attacker drive state-changing NodeGoat routes over the ci-to-app flow's HTTP endpoints
threats.asset: user profile data and session-backed account state
threats.attackScenario: The Express app reached over the ci-to-app HTTP flow authenticates with a cookie session (express-session at server.js:78) but registers no CSRF middleware for POST /login, POST /profile, POST /contributions, POST /benefits or POST /memos in app/routes/index.js, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to http://<host>:4000/profile and silently rewrites a logged-in victim's profile fields (or logs the victim into an attacker-controlled account via POST /login).
assumptions: The csurf dependency present in package.json is not wired up anywhere in the request pipeline at runtime.
Victims browse the application in the same browser session used for the attacker's page.
threats.impactReason: State-changing routes rewrite user profile and contribution records for any logged-in victim who visits an attacker page.
threats.likelihoodReason: The routes are plain cookie-authenticated form POSTs on a network-reachable HTTP port; no attacker position beyond a hosted page is needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already declared in package.json and emit tokens on every state-changing form.
steps: Uncomment and register `csrf` in server.js (line 7 shows the import already commented out) after the session middleware.
Add a hidden `_csrf` field to every POST form rendered by the swig views for /login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos.
Set SameSite=Lax (or Strict) on the express-session cookie in server.js:78 as defence in depth.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn reachable over the ci-to-app flow
threats.asset: user session credentials harvested via a phishing landing page
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list or validation, so an attacker mails a logged-in employee a link to http://<host>:4000/learn?url=https://nodegoat-login.attacker.tld and the victim lands on a cloned login page that captures their NodeGoat credentials.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or validates the url query parameter before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: The redirect launders an attacker domain behind the trusted application host, making credential phishing markedly more effective.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user clicking a crafted link triggers it; the parameter is fully attacker-controlled with no validation.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to an allow-list of known documentation URLs.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of req.query.url against a hardcoded map of permitted learning-resource destinations.
Return 400 for any value not in the map instead of redirecting.

threats.title: No security response headers on the application exposed by the ci-to-app flow
threats.asset: user profile data and application routes rendered in the victim's browser
threats.attackScenario: The Express app served over the ci-to-app HTTP flow registers no helmet or header middleware (helmet is imported only in a comment at server.js:10 and the header block at server.js:38-60 is commented out), so an attacker frames http://<host>:4000/profile in a transparent iframe on their own page and clickjacks a logged-in victim into submitting the profile update form, and any injected markup in the swig-rendered pages executes with no content security policy to stop it.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
No reverse proxy in front of the deployed app adds X-Frame-Options, CSP or HSTS.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP and frame protection remove the browser-side barriers that would otherwise blunt XSS and clickjacking against profile and memo pages.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every HTTP response over this flow lacks the headers, and framing or script-injection attacks need only a victim who visits an attacker page. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable the helmet middleware already listed in package.json for all responses.
steps: Uncomment `const helmet = require("helmet")` at server.js:10 and `app.use(helmet())` plus `app.disable("x-powered-by")` in the block at server.js:38-60.
Configure helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with an explicit script-src that excludes 'unsafe-inline'.
Enable helmet.hsts once the app is served over TLS.

threats.title: Cypress end-to-end specs drive the app over plaintext HTTP with a Secure-less session cookie on the ci-to-app flow
threats.asset: session cookies and the credentials posted to /login
threats.attackScenario: The ci-to-app flow is plain HTTP (server.js keeps the HTTPS key/cert loading commented out at lines 18-28) and the express-session cookie at server.js:78 is issued without the Secure attribute, so anyone able to observe the network path between the driving client and port 4000 reads the connect.sid value and the credentials submitted to POST /login, then replays the cookie to reach /profile and /allocations as that user.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating proxy sets the Secure flag on the session cookie.
The same HTTP-only configuration exercised by the CI run is used when the application is deployed beyond localhost, so traffic is observable by a network attacker.
threats.impactReason: A captured connect.sid grants full authenticated access to profile, contributions and allocations data for the victim account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Interception requires a position on the network path; within a CI runner that is limited, but the same plaintext configuration ships to any non-local deployment. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Uncomment the https server setup at server.js:18-28 and listen with https.createServer(httpsOptions, app) outside test runs.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax" }` on the express-session options at server.js:78, gated on NODE_ENV so the CI HTTP run still works.
Add helmet.hsts once TLS is in place.

threats.title: Missing ownership check on GET /allocations/:userId exposed through the ci-to-app flow
threats.asset: other users' retirement allocation records
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is guarded only by the isLoggedIn middleware with no comparison between :userId and the session user, so an attacker signs up via POST /signup, notes their own numeric userId from /allocations/<own id>, and iterates neighbouring ids over the same HTTP flow to read every other employee's allocation breakdown.
assumptions: No ownership filtering happens inside allocationsHandler.displayAllocations.
User ids are sequential integers assigned at signup, making neighbouring ids trivially guessable.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation record is enumerable one id at a time by any account holder.
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-service signup is open on the same flow and the only prerequisite is a logged-in session plus an id in the path.

mitigation.summary: Scope the allocations lookup to the session's user unless the caller is an admin.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:63 add the existing isAdmin middleware for cross-user lookups, or compare req.params.userId with req.session.userId in allocationsHandler.displayAllocations and return 404 on mismatch.
Apply the same check to any query issued against the allocations collection.

threats.title: CSRF lets an attacker change a victim's contribution percentages and trigger the eval() sink
threats.asset: payroll contribution percentages of the logged-in user
threats.attackScenario: With no CSRF token on POST /contributions and an express-session cookie that has no SameSite attribute, an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to http://nodegoat/contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth fields; a logged-in victim visiting it has their contribution record overwritten under their session userId, and the same cross-site POST reaches the eval() sink in app/routes/contributions.js.
assumptions: No CSRF token is validated by middleware upstream of the contributions routes.
threats.impactReason: Victim payroll contribution percentages are silently altered and the cross-site request can carry an eval payload executed server-side.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires the victim to be logged in and visit an attacker page; the session cookie has no SameSite restriction.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token protection for all state-changing routes, including POST /contributions.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware already listed in server.js:7 and server.js:107.
Expose res.locals.csrftoken and render it as a hidden field in app/views/contributions.html.
Set the session cookie SameSite attribute to 'lax' or 'strict' in the express-session options in server.js:78.

threats.title: MongoDB wire traffic from the contributions handler is unauthenticated and unencrypted across the container boundary
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB collections, including plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used at server.js:30 comes from MONGODB_URI, set in docker-compose.yml:8 to mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no username, password or TLS option, so anyone who reaches the docker network (a compromised sibling container or a host with the port exposed) reads and rewrites the contributions and users collections that the ContributionsDAO upsert traverses, or impersonates the application to the database.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the mongo container's network segment.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The deployed MONGODB_URI carries no credentials and no tls=true parameter, matching the docker-compose value.
threats.impactReason: Direct read/write access to collections holding plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank routing details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the container network, but no credential is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Create a least-privilege Mongo user and put its credentials in MONGODB_URI via a secret rather than in docker-compose.yml.
Append tls=true (and a CA file) to the connection string consumed by MongoClient.connect in server.js:30.
Enable authorization in the mongo service configuration so unauthenticated clients are rejected.

threats.title: Contribution upsert keyed by an unparsed userId can be steered to another user's document
threats.asset: other users' payroll contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: ContributionsDAO.update at app/data/contributions-dao.js:28 matches on the raw session userId while storing parsedUserId in the document, so a value that differs between its raw and parsed forms causes the upsert to miss the intended document and insert a new contributions record under a mismatched key, corrupting which user the percentages in the contributions collection belong to.
assumptions: req.session.userId can hold a non-canonical numeric form (for example a string) because no schema enforces its type.
threats.impactReason: Contribution records become attached to the wrong user key, letting one user's percentages be read or overwritten as another's.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the session userId to be stored in a non-canonical form; the mismatch is present in code on every write.

mitigation.summary: Use a single canonical userId type for both the query filter and the stored document.
steps: Change the filter in app/data/contributions-dao.js:28 to { userId: parsedUserId }.
Validate and coerce req.session.userId to an integer once at session creation and reject non-numeric values.

threats.title: Missing security response headers allow the contributions page to be framed and injected content to run
threats.asset: payroll contribution percentages and the victim's authenticated session actions
threats.attackScenario: GET /contributions renders the contributions view with no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options header, so an attacker frames the page on their own site and overlays a UI that tricks a logged-in user into submitting the contributions form, and any script that reaches the rendered template runs unrestricted and issues same-origin POSTs to /contributions on the victim's behalf.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the Express server adds the missing security headers.
threats.impactReason: Clickjacking and unrestricted script execution let an attacker perform contribution changes as the victim; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any user browsing to an attacker-controlled page while logged in is affected; no special position required.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet so Express emits CSP, frameguard and nosniff headers.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and the helmet middleware block at server.js:38-65.
Add helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with a policy that disallows inline script for the contributions views.
Call app.disable('x-powered-by') in server.js.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() of preTax/afterTax/roth on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the Node.js application process and everything it can reach, including the nodegoat MongoDB database
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user submits POST /contributions with preTax set to a JavaScript expression such as `require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString().length`, which app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 passes straight to eval() before any isNaN or range validation runs, giving the attacker arbitrary code execution inside the Express process and direct access to the connected MongoDB handle holding plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank details.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the application process exposes the whole database (plaintext passwords, SSN, bank details) and the host.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can post the form field; the expression is evaluated unconditionally before validation.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing and strict validation of the three contribution fields.
steps: Use the already-present commented alternative in app/routes/contributions.js:38-40: parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) etc.
Reject any value that is not a finite integer between 0 and 30 before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a regression test posting a JavaScript expression to POST /contributions and asserting a validation error.

threats.title: Contribution writes are not attributable because ContributionsDAO logs only a generic message
threats.asset: audit trail for payroll contribution changes
threats.attackScenario: After a CSRF-forced or eval-driven POST /contributions, ContributionsDAO.update at app/data/contributions-dao.js:36 records only "Updated contributions" with no userId, previous values, timestamp or source IP, so a user who changed their own percentages can deny doing so and an intruder's writes cannot be traced back.
assumptions: No external audit logging middleware records request bodies and identities for /contributions.
threats.impactReason: Disputes over payroll contribution changes cannot be resolved and attacker activity cannot be reconstructed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every write through this path is unattributed by default.

mitigation.summary: Write an auditable record for every contribution update.
steps: In app/data/contributions-dao.js:36 log userId, old and new preTax/afterTax/roth values and a timestamp instead of the bare message.
Persist the audit entries to a dedicated collection or append-only log store rather than stdout only.

threats.title: Infinite-loop or resource-exhaustion payload evaluated by POST /contributions eval()
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server
threats.attackScenario: An attacker posts preTax=while(1){} (or a huge Array allocation) to POST /contributions; app/routes/contributions.js:32 evaluates it with eval() on the single Node.js event loop thread, blocking the process so no other user request, including login, is served.
assumptions: The application runs as a single Node process without an external watchdog that restarts a blocked worker.
threats.impactReason: A single request permanently stalls the event loop, taking the whole application offline until it is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivial payload sent to a normal form endpoint reachable by any registered user.

mitigation.summary: Remove eval() so attacker-supplied strings are never executed.
steps: Parse contribution fields with parseInt/Number in app/routes/contributions.js instead of eval().
Add a request body size limit and a process supervisor that restarts an unresponsive worker.

threats.title: Unbounded contribution upserts through the MongoDB flow can exhaust database resources
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB instance
threats.attackScenario: An attacker scripts thousands of POST /contributions requests from a single logged-in session; each one issues a ContributionsDAO.update upsert over the MongoDB wire connection with no rate limit or connection-pool cap in front of it, saturating the mongo container and stalling every other DAO that shares the same connection.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request throttling is applied in front of the Express application or the MongoDB connection.
threats.impactReason: Database saturation takes down login, profile and benefits flows that share the same MongoClient connection.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a registered account and a simple request loop are needed.

mitigation.summary: Throttle state-changing requests and bound the MongoDB connection pool.
steps: Add per-session and per-IP rate limiting to POST /contributions in app/routes/index.js.
Set a maxPoolSize and serverSelectionTimeoutMS on MongoClient.connect in server.js:30 so a request storm fails fast instead of queueing.

threats.title: Mongo service runs without persistent volume or resource limits, allowing destructive reset and denial of service
threats.asset: stored nodegoat application data in MongoDB
threats.attackScenario: The web service command at docker-compose.yml:9 runs node artifacts/db-reset.js on every container start and the mongo service at docker-compose.yml:13-17 declares no volume, so an attacker who can trigger a container restart (for example by exhausting the unlimited memory of the mongo container with large inserts through the app) causes the database to be wiped and re-seeded, destroying all stored records.
assumptions: No external orchestration adds volumes or memory limits to the mongo service.
The compose stack is used beyond local throwaway testing, so loss of the mongo data directory is meaningful.
threats.impactReason: All persisted documents are lost on restart and no backup path is declared in the compose stack.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to force a restart or exhaust container resources, which is indirect.

mitigation.summary: Persist Mongo data and constrain container resources so a restart or resource exhaustion does not destroy data.
steps: Add a named volume to the mongo service in docker-compose.yml mapping /data/db.
Remove node artifacts/db-reset.js from the web service command at docker-compose.yml:9 for any non-test profile.
Set mem_limit and cpus on both the web and mongo services in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: MongoDB connection string in docker-compose.yml uses no authentication or TLS
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB database contents (user accounts, memos, allocations)
threats.attackScenario: The compose file sets MONGODB_URI to mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat at docker-compose.yml:8 with no username, password or tls option, so an attacker who obtains any foothold on the compose bridge network (for example by exploiting the web container exposed on port 4000) connects to the mongo service on 27017 with the mongo shell and reads or drops the nodegoat collections without credentials.
assumptions: The mongo:4.4 image is started without --auth, so the database accepts unauthenticated connections from the compose network.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated database access permits reading and modifying every document, including stored user records.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a position on the compose network or host, but no credential is needed once there.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and encrypted transport for the MongoDB service used by the web container.
steps: Add MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME and MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD to the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and start mongod with --auth.
Change MONGODB_URI at docker-compose.yml:8 to include the credentials and ?tls=true, sourcing the password from an environment file rather than the committed compose file.
Enable TLS on the mongod service and configure the mongodb driver (package.json dependency mongodb ^2.1.18) accordingly, or upgrade the driver to a version supporting current TLS options.

threats.title: Seeder writes fixed admin credentials to MongoDB over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: seeded default administrator credentials and the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The seeder connects using the `db` value from config/env/all.js:3, which defaults to `mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat` and is set in docker-compose.yml:8 to `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no username, password or TLS parameters, so an attacker with access to the compose network connects directly to mongo:27017, reads the `users` documents the seeder inserted (admin password and, per app/data/user-dao.js:25, plaintext passwords of real users) and rewrites `isAdmin: true` onto an account they control.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the compose network segment, for example from another container or a host with the port exposed.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The MongoDB deployment reachable at mongo:27017 accepts connections without authentication and without requiring TLS, as the connection string implies.
threats.impactReason: Direct read/write access to the users collection yields administrator credentials, plaintext user passwords and SSN/bank fields, and permits privilege escalation by flipping isAdmin.
threats.likelihoodReason: No credentials or TLS appear in the connection string, so any attacker who gains a foothold on the same network reaches the database with no further exploitation. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the seeder and the application.
steps: Enable MongoDB authentication on the `mongo` service in docker-compose.yml and create a least-privilege user for the nodegoat database.
Change MONGODB_URI to include credentials from a secret store and append `?tls=true` (or configure the driver's tls options) so the wire protocol is encrypted.
Remove the fallback literal `mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat` in config/env/all.js:3 and fail fast when MONGODB_URI is unset.

threats.title: Container start command reruns db-reset.js and destroys all collections on every restart
threats.asset: all stored user, allocation, contribution and memo documents in the nodegoat database
threats.attackScenario: The web service's compose command at docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start`, and that script calls tryDropCollection (artifacts/db-reset.js:39-48) against the shared mongo service; an attacker who can force the web container to restart (for example by crashing the Node process) causes every collection in the nodegoat database to be dropped and replaced by the three fixture accounts, wiping all real user allocations, contributions and memos.
assumptions: The same MongoDB instance defined as the `mongo` compose service also holds non-fixture data in a deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Dropping the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections destroys all application data and resets administrator credentials to known values.
threats.likelihoodReason: The destructive run is wired into the normal container start command and app.json postdeploy, so any restart or redeploy triggers it without an attacker needing privileged access.

mitigation.summary: Separate seeding from the container start path and guard it against non-development environments.
steps: Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js &&` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml:9 and invoke it only through an explicit `npm run db:seed` on demand.
Add an early guard in artifacts/db-reset.js that aborts unless NODE_ENV is development/test or an explicit ALLOW_DB_RESET flag is set.
Remove or gate the `postdeploy` hook in app.json:13 so production deploys never drop collections.

threats.title: Seeder drops and repopulates collections with no audit record of who reset the database
threats.asset: integrity record of the nodegoat users, allocations and memos collections
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js only prints `Dropped collection: <name>` to stdout (line 43) with no operator identity, timestamp or durable audit sink, so anyone able to run `npm run db:seed` or restart the web container can destroy the users collection and reinstate the fixed `admin` account, and afterwards nobody can attribute the reset to a particular actor.
assumptions: Container stdout is not shipped to a tamper-resistant audit log that records who invoked the seeder.
threats.impactReason: Loss of attribution for a full data-destroying and credential-resetting action hinders incident response, though it does not itself disclose data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone with shell or restart access to the web container can run the script, and the only trace is ephemeral console output.

mitigation.summary: Emit an attributable, durable audit record for every seeder invocation.
steps: In artifacts/db-reset.js, log invoking user, hostname, NODE_ENV and an ISO timestamp before dropping each collection instead of the bare console.log at line 43.
Write a marker document (operation, timestamp, invoker) into an append-only `audit` collection as the first seeder action.
Ship container stdout to an external log store so the record survives container replacement.

threats.title: Seeder connection loss or a flooded MongoDB leaves the application unable to start
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat application and its seeded accounts
threats.attackScenario: An attacker who can reach mongo:27017 on the compose network (the port is exposed to the network per docker-compose.yml:13-17) opens enough connections or issues expensive operations that the seeder's writes fail, causing parseResponse in artifacts/db-reset.js:50-56 to call process.exit(1); because the compose command at docker-compose.yml:9 chains `node artifacts/db-reset.js && npm start`, the web service never starts and the application stays down.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
MongoDB accepts connections from other containers on the compose network without authentication or connection limits.
threats.impactReason: The application cannot boot while the seeder fails, producing a full outage until an operator intervenes.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to already have network reach to the mongo service, but no credentials are needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Decouple application startup from the seeder and bound the seeder's database interaction.
steps: Split the compose command in docker-compose.yml:9 so `npm start` runs independently of the seeder's exit code.
Add connect and socket timeouts plus bounded retries to the MongoClient options in artifacts/db-reset.js rather than exiting on first error.
Restrict access to the mongo service to the web container only and enable MongoDB authentication and maxIncomingConnections.

threats.title: Web container publishes port 4000 on all host interfaces
threats.asset: application sessions and the data served by the nodegoat web application
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:11 maps "4000:4000" without a bind address and without any TLS terminator in the compose stack, so anyone who can reach the host on port 4000 speaks plain HTTP to the web service and can observe or replay the express-session cookie (set at server.js:78 with Secure off) from intercepted traffic to take over a logged-in session.
assumptions: The compose stack is run on a host reachable from an untrusted network with no reverse proxy terminating TLS in front of port 4000.
threats.impactReason: Plaintext exposure of the application allows session cookie capture and full impersonation of logged-in users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The port mapping is unconditional, but exploitation needs network reachability or an on-path position.

mitigation.summary: Bind the published port to localhost and terminate TLS in front of the web service.
steps: Change the ports entry at docker-compose.yml:11 to "127.0.0.1:4000:4000" so the container is not published on all host interfaces.
Add a TLS-terminating reverse proxy service to docker-compose.yml and route external traffic through it.
Set cookie.secure true for the express-session configuration at server.js:78 once TLS fronts the service.

threats.title: Unpinned third-party actions in the E2E workflow allow supply-chain tampering of the CI build
threats.asset: the CI build pipeline and its runner environment (npm cache, GITHUB_TOKEN)
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test job at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:5 consumes actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 by mutable tag rather than by commit SHA, so an attacker who compromises one of those action repositories (or a maintainer account able to move the v2 tag) publishes a new commit under the same tag and executes arbitrary code inside the ubuntu-latest runner on every push, tampering with the checked-out source before `npm ci` runs and reading runner secrets.
assumptions: The referenced action tags are mutable and are resolved at run time rather than being pinned by an organisation-level policy.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code in the runner can alter build artefacts and read any secret exposed to the job.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromising a widely-watched GitHub-owned action repository or its tags, which is uncommon though repeatedly demonstrated.

mitigation.summary: Pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA and restrict workflow permissions.
steps: Replace `uses: actions/checkout@v2`, `actions/setup-node@v1` and `actions/cache@v2` in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml with `uses: actions/<name>@<40-char commit SHA>` and record the version in a trailing comment.
Add a top-level `permissions: contents: read` block to the workflow so the job token cannot write to the repository.
Enable Dependabot for GitHub Actions to keep the pinned SHAs updated.

threats.title: Cache poisoning of the shared npm cache in the E2E workflow
threats.asset: npm dependencies installed into the CI build (~/.npm, ~/.cache)
threats.attackScenario: The workflow triggers on `pull_request` (.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:2) and restores ~/.npm and ~/.cache keyed only on runner OS, node version and hashFiles('package-lock.json') at line 31, so an attacker opens a pull request from a fork whose branch writes a tampered package tarball into that cache key, and the subsequent `npm ci` on the default branch restores the poisoned entry and installs attacker-controlled module code into the build.
assumptions: Cache entries written by pull-request runs of this workflow are readable by runs on the base branch, i.e. no cache-scope isolation is configured for the repository.
threats.impactReason: Poisoned dependencies execute in the CI runner and can corrupt test results or exfiltrate the runner environment, though the cache is scoped to this repository.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a fork pull request and a cache-key collision; GitHub's branch-scoped cache isolation limits but does not fully prevent it.
