Combine with the host allow-list so only the pinned quote provider can be contacted.

threats.title: Session cookie and rendered PII exposed on plaintext HTTP to the browser
threats.asset: the express-session cookie and the SSN, date of birth and bank account and routing numbers rendered into app/views/profile.html
threats.attackScenario: The views-to-user flow is described as HTTP and the express-session cookie at server.js:78 is issued without the Secure attribute, so an attacker on the same network as a user browsing /profile captures the session cookie and the plaintext HTML containing the SSN, DOB and bank account and routing number field values, then replays the cookie to impersonate the victim; the same position lets them rewrite the delivered HTML to alter the POST /profile form target.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reached over plain HTTP in at least some deployments, or is not fronted by a TLS-terminating proxy that also sets HSTS.
The session cookie is sent on requests to the pages rendered from app/views.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie yields full account takeover, and the same traffic carries SSN, date of birth and bank account and routing numbers in cleartext.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position such as shared Wi-Fi or an upstream hop, but no authentication or application-level foothold. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve all views over TLS and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' } on the express-session configuration at server.js:78.
Redirect all plain HTTP requests to HTTPS and send Strict-Transport-Security (helmet.hsts covers this once helmet is added).
Verify the deployment terminates TLS in front of the Express process before enabling secure cookies.

threats.title: Missing security response headers on HTML delivered to the browser
threats.asset: rendered user data including SSN, date of birth and bank account and routing numbers shown on /profile
threats.attackScenario: Responses rendered from app/views are sent with no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options header, so an attacker who lands any script into a page (for example through the memo Markdown on /memos) faces no CSP to block inline execution or exfiltration to an external host, and can additionally frame /profile and /benefits on an attacker-controlled page to clickjack the victim into submitting those forms.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or CDN in front of the Express app adds these headers before the response reaches the browser.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP and frame protections remove the defence-in-depth layer that would otherwise contain script injection and framing of the profile and benefits forms.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every HTML response from the application is affected and reachable by any browser client with no special position.

mitigation.summary: Add helmet and set a restrictive Content-Security-Policy for rendered views.
steps: Install and mount helmet in the Express app so X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy are sent on all responses.
Configure helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with default-src 'self' and no 'unsafe-inline', moving inline <style> blocks such as the one in app/views/login.html:19 into the existing /vendor CSS files.
Set frame-ancestors 'none' so /profile and /benefits cannot be framed.

threats.title: Stored XSS through memo content rendered as raw Markdown HTML in app/views/memos.html
threats.asset: rendered user data and the victim's authenticated session actions (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers shown on /profile)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker posts a memo to POST /memos containing Markdown that embeds raw HTML such as ; app/views/memos.html line 31 renders {{ marked(doc.memo) }}, and because marked() returns HTML the payload executes in every other user's browser when they open /memos, letting the script read the victim's /profile page (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers) and submit forms such as POST /profile or POST /benefits as the victim.
assumptions: Memos written by one user are displayed to other users on /memos.

marked() is invoked with HTML sanitisation disabled (the default for marked) and Swig does not escape the value returned by the marked filter/function, so stored memo HTML reaches the browser unescaped.
threats.impactReason: Script running in a victim's session can read the profile page containing SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers and can perform state-changing POSTs as that user; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly so it cannot be read by the script.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can submit a memo through the textarea on /memos and the payload is stored and replayed to every reader with no filtering step in the template.

mitigation.summary: Sanitise memo Markdown output before it is rendered as HTML.
steps: Configure marked with sanitisation or pass its output through a sanitiser (for example DOMPurify/sanitize-html) in the memos handler before passing memosList to the view.
In app/views/memos.html line 31, render the pre-sanitised HTML variable rather than calling marked() on raw stored content in the template.
Restrict allowed Markdown output to a safe tag/attribute allowlist that excludes script, iframe, and on* event handlers.

threats.title: Arbitrary local file read via vulnerable swig@1.4.2 template rendering (CVE-2023-25345)
threats.asset: arbitrary server-side files readable by the Node process, including app/data configuration and credentials
threats.attackScenario: swig@1.4.2 is declared in package.json:22 and is affected by CVE-2023-25345; wherever a template name or include/extends path is influenced by request data, an attacker supplies a traversal path (for example ../../../../etc/passwd) so that the Swig renderer used by consolidate reads and returns that local file in the HTTP response instead of an app/views template.
assumptions: At least one render/include path in the application is derived from user-controlled input, which is required to reach the vulnerable code path.
No fixed swig release exists, so the dependency remains exploitable until replaced.
threats.impactReason: Reading arbitrary server files exposes application configuration and database credentials used by the rest of the system.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable version is pinned and unfixed, but exploitation depends on a user-controllable template path, which is not demonstrated in the views themselves.

mitigation.summary: Replace the unmaintained swig renderer and never derive template paths from request input.
steps: Migrate app/views templates to a maintained engine (for example nunjucks, whose syntax is closest to Swig) and update the consolidate engine registration.
Audit all res.render calls so the template name is a fixed literal chosen from an allowlist, never concatenated from req params or query values.
Remove swig from package.json once the migration is complete.

threats.title: Raw error object printed to the browser by app/views/error-template.html
threats.asset: stack-trace / error output revealing file paths, query structure and dependency versions
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sends malformed input to a route such as GET /allocations/{{userId}}?threshold=' (or any value that makes the Mongo query throw) and reads the response body rendered by app/views/error-template.html line 11, which prints {{error}} verbatim, harvesting absolute server file paths, driver stack frames and query fragments to target follow-up injection attempts.
assumptions: The error handler passes the raw Error/stack object into the `error` template variable in all environments rather than a generic message in production.
threats.impactReason: Stack traces disclose internal paths, library versions and query shapes that materially assist injection and dependency-targeted attacks, but no user records are directly exposed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Triggering an application error only requires sending unexpected input to a reachable route, and the template unconditionally prints the error value.

mitigation.summary: Render a generic message to users and log the error server-side.
steps: Change app/views/error-template.html line 11 to a static message such as 'An internal error occurred' plus a correlation id.
In the Express error handler, log the full error to the server log and pass only the correlation id into the template.
Ensure the stack is never added to the template context when NODE_ENV is production.

threats.title: IDOR on GET /allocations/:userId lets any logged-in user read other users' allocations and names
threats.asset: per-user asset allocation records and user names
threats.attackScenario: An attacker registers an account, logs in, then changes the path parameter on the browser-to-handler flow from /allocations/<own id> to /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on; app/routes/allocations.js reads userId from req.params with the session-based fix commented out at lines 13-18, so the DAO returns another user's stocks/funds/bonds plus firstName and lastName rendered in allocations.html.
assumptions: Numeric user ids are sequential and therefore trivially enumerable.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation record and real name can be harvested one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, authenticated user reaches the route and only has to edit a URL path segment.

mitigation.summary: Derive the user id from the session rather than the URL path.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;` as the commented fix at lines 13-15 indicates.
If the path parameter must remain for bookmarking, compare req.params.userId against req.session.userId and return 404 when they differ.

threats.title: Session cookie for the allocations request travels over plaintext HTTP and can be replayed
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: An attacker on the same Wi-Fi as an employee captures the plaintext GET /allocations/:userId request on port 4000 — server.js:145 starts an http server and the session cookie at server.js:78 is configured without `secure` — then replays the connect.sid value to fetch /allocations pages and the victim's profile as that user.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reached directly over http://host:4000 with no TLS-terminating reverse proxy in front of it.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full authenticated access to the victim's account, including SSN, date of birth and bank account fields on the profile page.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position such as shared Wi-Fi or a compromised hop, but no application-level exploit. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 (and the key/cert loading at lines 18-28) and stop listening on plain http at line 145.
Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Add HSTS, for example by re-enabling helmet.hsts() in the block at server.js:38-65.

threats.title: Missing CSRF tokens and security headers on the allocations flow allow forged and clickjacked requests
threats.asset: per-user asset allocation records
threats.attackScenario: With csurf commented out at server.js:7/104-113 and no SameSite attribute on the session cookie, an attacker hosts a page that frames or auto-submits requests to http://host:4000/allocations/... and to the state-changing POST routes of the same session; because no X-Frame-Options or CSP is set, the victim's browser attaches the session cookie and the attacker drives actions in the employee's logged-in session.
assumptions: A victim with an active NodeGoat session visits an attacker-controlled page while logged in.
Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
threats.impactReason: State-changing actions can be performed as the victim, and framed pages allow allocation data to be read or acted upon via clickjacking.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated employee to a web page; no network position or credentials needed. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and security response headers.
steps: Uncomment the csurf setup at server.js:104-113 and emit {{csrftoken}} as a hidden field in the forms under app/views/.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true }` in the express-session config at server.js:78.
Re-enable helmet with frameguard and contentSecurityPolicy as sketched at server.js:38-65 and add helmet to package.json dependencies.

threats.title: NoSQL $where injection through the threshold query parameter on the allocations request
threats.asset: all allocations documents in MongoDB and application availability
threats.attackScenario: The attacker submits the allocations form or calls GET /allocations/1?threshold=1'; return 1 == '1 ; app/data/allocations-dao.js:77-79 interpolates the raw threshold string into a `$where` JavaScript expression, so the injected predicate returns every allocations document regardless of userId, and a payload such as 0';while(true){}' hangs the MongoDB server-side JavaScript evaluation and stalls the database.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment has server-side JavaScript evaluation enabled so that $where expressions execute.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary JavaScript in the query predicate exposes the whole allocations collection and can lock the database in an infinite loop.
threats.likelihoodReason: The threshold field is a free-text input in allocations.html:22 (the numeric-validation input is commented out) and reachable by any authenticated user.

mitigation.summary: Stop building a $where expression from user input on the threshold parameter.
steps: In app/data/allocations-dao.js:57-84 replace the `$where` branch with a plain comparison query such as `{ userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }`.
Parse threshold with parseInt(threshold, 10) and reject values outside 0-99 before querying, as the commented block at lines 70-75 shows.
Restore the numeric input `<input type="number" min="0" max="99" ...>` in app/views/allocations.html:21 for defence in depth.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery against POST /login allows login CSRF and forced session fixation
threats.asset: the victim's session and the profile data (SSN, bank account and routing numbers) they subsequently enter
threats.attackScenario: No CSRF middleware runs in front of POST /login at app/routes/index.js:34 and the session cookie has no SameSite attribute, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form of their own credentials to http://nodegoat/login, silently logging the victim into the attacker's account so that SSN and bank details the victim then types into /profile are stored in the attacker's record.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds SameSite to the session cookie.
The application is reachable by a browser that has been lured to an attacker-controlled page.
threats.impactReason: Data the victim enters afterwards lands in an attacker-controlled account, and the victim's own session can be replaced without their knowledge.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring a victim to a page, but no authentication or privileged position is needed by the attacker.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already declared as a dependency and add SameSite to the session cookie.
steps: Uncomment the csrf() registration and the res.locals.csrftoken middleware at server.js:104-113 (csurf is already in package.json:11).
Render {{csrftoken}} as a hidden input in app/views/login.html and app/views/signup.html and verify it on POST /login and POST /signup.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'lax' }` in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Login and signup credentials travel over plaintext HTTP and the session cookie is not marked Secure
threats.asset: user credentials and the express-session session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the application with http.createServer (the https.createServer block at lines 149-155 is commented out) and the express-session configuration at server.js:78 leaves the cookie options block commented out so `secure` stays false, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a victim sniffs the POST /login body (app/routes/index.js:34) to read the plaintext username and password and replays the connect.sid cookie to take over the session.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reached directly over HTTP rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy that also rewrites cookie flags.
threats.impactReason: Credentials and the session identifier for accounts holding SSN, date of birth and bank account numbers are exposed in cleartext.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any network-path observer on an untrusted network captures the POST body without needing an account. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie Secure and HttpOnly.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 and remove the plaintext http.createServer listener at server.js:145, or terminate TLS at the proxy and set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`.
Uncomment the cookie option block in the session() call at server.js:92-100 and set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' }`.
Add helmet.hsts() (helmet is already a dependency in package.json:16) so browsers refuse to downgrade.

threats.title: Unauthenticated password guessing against POST /login
threats.asset: user accounts and the SSN, date of birth and bank account numbers they hold
threats.attackScenario: POST /login at app/routes/index.js:34 accepts unlimited attempts from one source, so an attacker scripts a loop posting userName and password pairs from a leaked credential list until a response redirects to /dashboard, then reads the victim's SSN and bank routing number from /profile.
assumptions: Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
No rate limiting, lockout or CAPTCHA is applied in front of POST /login by the application or any fronting proxy.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password yields full account takeover including SSN, date of birth and bank account details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The endpoint is unauthenticated, cheap to call and needs no special position. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and lock out repeated failed logins on POST /login.
steps: Add an express rate-limiting middleware in front of app.post("/login") in app/routes/index.js:34, keyed by source IP and submitted userName.
Record consecutive failures per account in the users collection and refuse authentication for a cooling-off period after a threshold.
Log failed authentication attempts with source IP so brute force is visible.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let injected markup run in the login and signup pages
threats.asset: user credentials submitted on the login and signup forms
threats.attackScenario: No helmet middleware is registered (the helmet block at server.js:38-65 is commented out) so responses for GET /login and GET /signup carry no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options and no nosniff; an attacker frames http://nodegoat/login in a transparent iframe on their own page and clickjacks the victim into submitting the form, or injects a script tag through the unescaped signup error fields at app/views/signup.html:57 (swig autoescape is disabled at server.js:135-142) that posts the typed username and password to an external host.
assumptions: The application is served without a reverse proxy that injects CSP or frame-ancestors headers.
threats.impactReason: Credentials entered on the login form can be captured or the form submitted under the attacker's control, reaching accounts holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login and signup pages are unauthenticated and reachable by anyone, and no header blocks framing or foreign script sources.

mitigation.summary: Register helmet with a content security policy, frameguard and nosniff, and re-enable template autoescaping.
steps: Uncomment the helmet block at server.js:38-65 so helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.frameguard() and the nosniff middleware are applied (helmet is already in package.json:16).
Set swig autoescape back to true at server.js:135-142 so the error fields rendered in app/views/signup.html:57 are escaped.
Call app.disable('x-powered-by') as shown at server.js:42.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on POST /benefits changes another employee's benefit start date
threats.asset: employees' benefit start dates
threats.attackScenario: No CSRF token is issued or checked for the form in app/views/benefits.html:54 that posts to /benefits, and the express-session cookie carries no SameSite attribute, so an attacker lures a logged-in employee to a page that auto-submits a hidden form with userId and benefitStartDate to http://nodegoat/benefits, silently rewriting that employee record through app/data/benefits-dao.js:23.
assumptions: A logged-in user can be lured to an attacker-controlled page while holding a valid session cookie.
Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
No proxy adds a SameSite attribute to the session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates of arbitrary employees are silently modified with no record of who initiated the change.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an authenticated victim to visit an attacker page, but the request itself needs no token or referrer. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable csurf and emit a CSRF token in the benefits form.
steps: Uncomment the csrf() registration at server.js:104-113 (csurf is already declared in package.json:11).
Add a hidden csrftoken input to the form at app/views/benefits.html:54 and let csurf reject posts without it.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'strict' }` in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee can read the full roster and rewrite any employee's benefit start date via /benefits
threats.asset: all employees' benefit start dates and the non-admin employee roster
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:55-56 guards GET /benefits and POST /benefits with isLoggedIn only, with the isAdmin variant left commented out at lines 57-60, and app/routes/benefits.js:19-25 hardcodes user.isAdmin = true in the render context, so any self-registered user browses to /benefits, reads every non-admin employee's id and name from benefitsDAO.getAllNonAdminUsers, then posts userId and benefitStartDate for a colleague, which app/data/benefits-dao.js:23-30 writes straight into that user's document.
assumptions: Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.
The isLoggedIn middleware only establishes that a session exists and performs no role check.
threats.impactReason: The whole employee roster is disclosed and any employee's benefit start date can be altered by a non-privileged user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Signup is open and the route needs only a logged-in session, reached by typing the URL. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require the admin role on both /benefits routes and stop forcing isAdmin in the view model.
steps: Restore the commented-out admin-guarded routes at app/routes/index.js:57-60 so isAdmin runs after isLoggedIn on GET and POST /benefits.
Remove the hardcoded `user: { isAdmin: true }` from both render calls in app/routes/benefits.js and pass the real session user.
Validate that the posted userId exists and that benefitStartDate parses as a date before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.

threats.title: Employee roster and benefit data transit /benefits without TLS or anti-framing headers
threats.asset: the non-admin employee roster rendered by /benefits
threats.attackScenario: GET /benefits at app/routes/index.js:55 returns every non-admin employee's id, first name, last name and benefit start date (app/views/benefits.html:47-57) over the plaintext listener created at server.js:145, and with no helmet frameguard or CSP registered an attacker on the victim's network reads the roster off the wire, or frames the page on their own site and clickjacks the employee into pressing Save on a pre-filled benefit date.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The /benefits page is served over plaintext HTTP with no TLS-terminating proxy and no proxy-injected frame-ancestors or CSP header.
threats.impactReason: The full employee roster is disclosed to a network observer and benefit records can be altered through a framed page.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires either a network position or luring an authenticated employee, but no credentials of the attacker's own. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve /benefits over HTTPS and register helmet frameguard, HSTS and CSP.
steps: Switch the listener at server.js:145 to the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155.
Uncomment app.use(helmet.frameguard()), helmet.hsts() and helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() at server.js:44-54.
Uncomment app.use(helmet.noCache()) at server.js:48 so the roster page is not written to browser cache.

threats.title: Contribution values and session cookie sent over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie and submitted payroll contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: A network attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a user reads the POST /contributions request body and the connect.sid cookie in the clear, then replays the cookie to impersonate the user and submit their own preTax value to the eval()-backed handler.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reached directly over HTTP with no TLS-terminating proxy in front of it, and the session cookie is sent without the Secure attribute.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full account takeover, including the profile page holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires attacker presence on the network path, but no application-level obstacle exists once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie Secure with HSTS.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block already present in server.js:152 and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set cookie.secure = true in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Enable helmet.hsts() as sketched at server.js:54.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery forces a victim's contribution update, reaching the eval() sink
threats.asset: payroll contribution percentages and, via eval(), server-side code execution in the victim's session
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /contributions with chosen preTax/afterTax/roth values; because no CSRF token is required on the route registered at app/routes/index.js and the express-session cookie has no SameSite attribute, the victim's browser attaches the session cookie and the handler applies the attacker's values (and evaluates them) as that user.
assumptions: The victim is browsing with an active NodeGoat session cookie when they load the attacker's page.
threats.impactReason: The attacker changes the victim's payroll contributions and can drive attacker-chosen strings into the eval() calls in the victim's authenticated context.
threats.likelihoodReason: No token is required and the session cookie carries no SameSite restriction, so any lured page can issue the POST.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens for the contributions form and harden the session cookie.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware already present in server.js:107 and expose res.locals.csrftoken to templates.
Add a hidden _csrf input to the contributions form template.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } in the express-session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through POST /contributions preTax, afterTax and roth fields
threats.asset: the Node.js process and the MongoDB data it holds, including SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: A logged-in user submits the /contributions form with preTax set to a payload such as `global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd')` (or an infinite loop / `while(1){}`), and app/routes/contributions.js lines 32-34 pass the raw req.body values straight into eval(), executing attacker-supplied JavaScript inside the Express process with full access to the Mongo connection holding user SSNs and bank numbers.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the application process exposes every collection, including users' SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers, and allows full host compromise.
threats.likelihoodReason: The payload is a plain form field on a reachable POST route with no sanitisation between req.body and eval().

mitigation.summary: Stop evaluating request data as code; parse the contribution percentages numerically.
steps: Replace the three eval() calls at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 with parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) etc., as the commented-out block at lines 38-40 already shows.
Reject any value that is not an integer between 0 and 30 before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a lint rule (no-eval) so eval() cannot be reintroduced.

threats.title: Denial of service by supplying a blocking expression to the eval()'d contribution fields
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server for all users
threats.attackScenario: An attacker POSTs to /contributions with preTax=`while(true){}` (or `process.exit()`), which app/routes/contributions.js:32 evaluates on the single-threaded event loop, hanging or killing the server so no other user can reach any route.
threats.impactReason: One request permanently blocks the single Node event loop, taking down the whole application until it is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single form POST from any registered user triggers it; no tooling or special position is required.

mitigation.summary: Remove eval() from the contributions update path so request data can never be executed.
steps: Parse preTax, afterTax and roth with parseInt in app/routes/contributions.js before validation.
Add a process supervisor and request timeout so a single handler cannot stall the event loop indefinitely.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery posts memos as a victim user
threats.asset: memo content shared between all users
threats.attackScenario: An attacker lures a logged-in user to a page that auto-submits a form to POST /memos with a chosen `memo` field; with no CSRF token on the route registered at app/routes/index.js and no SameSite attribute on the express-session cookie, the memo is stored and displayed to every user as if the victim wrote it.
assumptions: The victim has an active NodeGoat session cookie while visiting the attacker's page.
threats.impactReason: Attacker-chosen content is injected into the shared memo board attributed to the victim's session, affecting all users who view /memos.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single auto-submitting form on any attacker-controlled page suffices; no token or origin check blocks it.

mitigation.summary: Require a CSRF token on POST /memos and restrict the session cookie with SameSite.
steps: Enable the csurf middleware commented out at server.js:107 and publish res.locals.csrftoken.
Add a hidden _csrf field to the memo form in app/views/memos.html.
Set cookie: { sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true, secure: true } in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Memo submissions and session cookie travel unencrypted over HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie and submitted memo content
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sniffing the network path reads the POST /memos body and the connect.sid session cookie in cleartext, or rewrites the `memo` field in transit to store content of their choosing on the shared memo board.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is served directly over HTTP with no TLS terminator in front, and the session cookie lacks the Secure attribute.
threats.impactReason: Capturing the session cookie yields account takeover, exposing the profile data (SSN, DOB, bank details) behind that session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position on the victim's path; no application control resists it once obtained. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS for all traffic and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block at server.js:152 and disable the plain http listener at server.js:145.
Set cookie.secure = true in the express-session configuration at server.js:78.
Add helmet.hsts() so browsers refuse plaintext on subsequent visits.

threats.title: Missing Content-Security-Policy leaves the memo page's rendered markdown without a script containment fallback
threats.asset: memo content shared between all users and the authenticated session context of every memo viewer
threats.attackScenario: An attacker POSTs a memo whose markdown embeds raw HTML/script; the stored memo is rendered for every other user at app/views/memos.html line 31 with swig autoescape disabled, and because no Content-Security-Policy or frame-ancestors header is emitted by the Express app, nothing stops the injected script from running in the viewer's origin, issuing same-origin requests such as POST /contributions on their behalf.
assumptions: The memo sanitisation applied by the marked library does not strip the injected markup for every payload variant.
threats.impactReason: Script running in a viewer's session can drive any state-changing route as them, including the eval()-backed /contributions handler; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly so it cannot be read by script.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any user can post a memo that all other users render, but success depends on bypassing the markdown sanitiser.

mitigation.summary: Add security response headers, notably a Content-Security-Policy, and re-enable template autoescaping.
steps: Enable the helmet middleware commented out at server.js:10 and server.js:45-54, including helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and frameguard.
Set swig autoescape back to true at server.js:137 so {{ }} output is escaped.
Sanitise memo HTML server-side before storage in app/data/memos-dao.js insert().

threats.title: POST /profile accepts cross-site forged submissions that overwrite SSN and bank details
threats.asset: the victim's stored SSN, date of birth, address and bank account/routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: The user-to-profile flow carries a cookie-authenticated form POST to /profile (app/routes/index.js:48) with no CSRF token in app/views/profile.html and no CSRF middleware in the request path, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to http://target/profile with firstName, ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting fields; a logged-in victim visiting it has their profile record silently rewritten by the attacker's values.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured for the express-session cookie.
threats.impactReason: The attacker rewrites the victim's financial identity fields (SSN, bank account and routing number) held against their account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user who loads an attacker page triggers it; the form is a plain urlencoded POST requiring no special privilege.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation for the /profile POST and mark the session cookie SameSite.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware and the res.locals.csrftoken helper in server.js (lines 7 and 104-113).
Add <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="{{csrftoken}}"> to the form in app/views/profile.html.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'strict', secure: true } on the express-session options in server.js:78.

threats.title: SSN, bank account and session cookie travel in cleartext HTTP on the profile submission
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers, and the session cookie in transit
threats.attackScenario: The user-to-profile flow is declared as HTTP and the express-session cookie at server.js:78 is configured without the Secure attribute, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as the victim captures the POST /profile body containing ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting together with the session cookie, then replays the cookie to impersonate the victim.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reached over plain HTTP in deployment rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy that also rewrites the cookie as Secure.
threats.impactReason: Full financial identity data plus a replayable session identifier are exposed to anyone on the network path.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position such as shared Wi-Fi or an upstream hop, but no application-level exploit. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block already present in server.js (lines 149-155) and redirect all plain HTTP requests to HTTPS.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } on the express-session options at server.js:78.
Add HSTS via helmet.hsts() as sketched at server.js:54.

threats.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking on the bankRouting field stalls the Node event loop
threats.asset: availability of the single-threaded Express server handling all user requests
threats.attackScenario: The bankRouting value carried on the user-to-profile flow is tested against /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59, so an attacker submits POST /profile with bankRouting=11111111111111111111111111111111111x and the nested quantifier backtracks exponentially, pinning the event loop and blocking every other request to the application.
threats.impactReason: Node.js runs one event loop, so a single crafted field makes the entire application unresponsive to all users until the regex completes.
threats.likelihoodReason: The field is a plain form input on a reachable POST route and the payload is a trivial digit string; repeated submissions keep the process saturated.

mitigation.summary: Replace the nested-quantifier regex with a linear-time validation of the routing number.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to /^[0-9]+#$/ (drop the outer + quantifier).
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum length before running any regex.

threats.title: Upstream response body written verbatim into the /research page with no CSP
threats.asset: the victim's authenticated session actions in the browser (same-origin requests such as POST /profile)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sends a victim a link to GET /research?url=https://attacker.test/&symbol=payload; app/routes/research.js:16-25 writes the attacker-controlled response body into a text/html response on the application's own origin, and with no Content-Security-Policy header set (helmet is commented out in server.js) the injected script runs same-origin and submits POST /profile as the victim to rewrite their SSN and bank details.
assumptions: The victim follows the crafted /research link while holding a valid session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Script executing on the application origin can drive any state-changing route as the victim; the session cookie itself is HttpOnly so it is the victim's actions, not the cookie, that are abused.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs the victim to open an attacker-supplied URL, but the injection itself requires no authentication or special position.

mitigation.summary: Stop echoing upstream bodies and add a restrictive Content-Security-Policy.
steps: Replace res.write(body) in app/routes/research.js:25 with rendering of parsed, escaped fields through the research template.
Enable helmet and helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() in server.js (lines 10 and 38-65) with a default-src 'self' policy.
Set swig autoescape back to true in server.js:135-142.

threats.title: Tutorial pages served over plaintext HTTP allow injection of attacker script into the same origin as the authenticated app
threats.asset: session cookie and user credentials submitted on the same origin
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the HTTPS block at server.js:149-155 is commented out, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a user browsing GET /tutorial/a1 (app/routes/tutorial.js:31) rewrites the plaintext HTML response of the tutorial page to add a script or a fake login form pointing at /login, and then captures the user's credentials and the connect.sid cookie, which is sent without the Secure attribute over the same cleartext channel.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
The application is reached directly over HTTP rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
threats.impactReason: A tampered tutorial page runs in the same origin as /profile and /allocations, and the plaintext channel also exposes the session cookie, reaching SSN, date of birth and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: The tutorial routes are unauthenticated and fetched by any visitor, but the attacker needs a network position between browser and server. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve all traffic, including /tutorial, over TLS and mark the session cookie Secure.
steps: Uncomment and use the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 (or terminate TLS at a proxy) and stop listening on plain HTTP.
Add an HSTS response header and redirect any http:// request to https://.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } in the express-session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Unauthenticated, uncached tutorial page rendering can be used to exhaust the single Node process
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy application to logged-in users
threats.attackScenario: GET /tutorial and GET /tutorial/<page> (app/routes/tutorial.js:8 and :31) render large Swig templates on every request with no authentication and no caching or request limiting, so an attacker loops thousands of concurrent requests against /tutorial/a1 … /tutorial/ssrf and saturates the single-threaded Express process, denying /login and /profile to real users.
assumptions: No rate limiting or reverse-proxy caching sits in front of the tutorial routes.
threats.impactReason: Loss of availability only; no data is disclosed or altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: The routes need no credentials and are trivially discoverable from the login page link.

mitigation.summary: Rate limit and cache the static tutorial responses.
steps: Put the pre-rendered tutorial pages behind express.static or a cache layer so each request does not re-render a template.
Add a per-IP request limiter in front of the /tutorial router mounted at app/routes/index.js:79.

threats.title: State-changing POSTs carried over the zap-to-app flow have no CSRF token, allowing forged profile updates
threats.asset: user profile data and session state
threats.attackScenario: The cookie session issued by express-session at server.js:78 has SameSite unset and no CSRF middleware guards app.post("/login") at app/routes/index.js:34 or app.post("/profile"), so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to http://<app>/profile and overwrites the victim's bank account and address fields, or logs the victim into an attacker-controlled account via the forged /login POST.
assumptions: The victim's browser sends the session cookie on cross-site POSTs because no SameSite attribute is applied by the deployment.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can silently change a victim's stored profile details, including payment-related fields, or pin the victim into an attacker session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires the logged-in victim to visit an attacker page; csurf is already a dependency but is not wired up.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation on all state-changing routes.
steps: Uncomment the csurf require at server.js:7 and register app.use(csrf()) before the routes are mounted.
Emit the token into every form template and validate it on POST /login, /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos.
Set cookie: { sameSite: "lax", secure: true, httpOnly: true } on the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: ZAP API key committed in config/env/development.js and config/env/test.js allows control of the ZAP proxy
threats.asset: ZAP API key and the ZAP scan results/proxy control it grants
threats.attackScenario: config/env/development.js:6 and config/env/test.js:6 hold a literal zapApiKey alongside the fixed zapHostName 192.168.56.20 and zapPort 8080, so anyone who reads the repository can call the ZAP API at http://192.168.56.20:8080 with that key (as test/security/profile-test.js:28 does) to read scan results for the /profile route, rewrite proxy rules, or start scans against arbitrary targets.
assumptions: A ZAP instance reachable at the configured host and port is running when a developer or CI job uses these config files.
The redacted zapApiKey values are real, non-placeholder keys committed to the repository.
threats.impactReason: The key grants API control of the ZAP proxy, which sees and can modify all proxied traffic including the test user's session, and exposes vulnerability scan results for the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The key is in source control and the endpoint address is fixed, but reaching 192.168.56.20:8080 normally requires being on the developer or CI network.

mitigation.summary: Remove the ZAP API key from committed config and load it from the environment.
steps: Replace the literal zapApiKey in config/env/development.js and config/env/test.js with process.env.ZAP_API_KEY.
Rotate the ZAP API key in ZAP Options -> API and bind the ZAP listener to localhost or an access-controlled interface.
Purge the committed key from git history.

threats.title: ZAP proxy sits in the clear on the path from the test browser to the application and can be impersonated
threats.asset: the test user's session cookie and /profile form credentials proxied through ZAP
threats.attackScenario: test/security/profile-test.js:18-21 and :55-57 point the Selenium browser's HTTP proxy at config.zapHostName:config.zapPort with sutProtocol "http://", so an attacker on the 192.168.56.0/24 segment who ARP-spoofs or binds 192.168.56.20:8080 first receives the plaintext login POST for sutUserName user1 and the resulting connect.sid cookie used to reach /profile.
assumptions: The ZAP proxy and the application under test are not confined to a loopback-only or otherwise isolated network when the security regression tests run.
threats.impactReason: Credentials and session cookies of the test account plus full request/response bodies for the /profile route are exposed to whoever holds the proxy position.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires presence on the same lab network as the ZAP host; it is a test-only path rather than an internet-facing one.

mitigation.summary: Run the ZAP proxy and system under test on an isolated or loopback network and use non-production test credentials.
steps: Bind ZAP to 127.0.0.1 and run the Selenium test against a local ZAP instance rather than the fixed 192.168.56.20 address in config/env/test.js.
Use throwaway credentials for sutUserName/sutUserPassword in test/security/profile-test.js and never reuse real accounts.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn reached over the zap-to-app flow
threats.asset: application routes and the trust users place in them (credential phishing)
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker sends a logged-in user http://<app>/learn?url=https://evil.example/login and the application bounces them to a look-alike login page that harvests their NodeGoat credentials.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or validates the url query parameter before the /learn handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Redirects away from a trusted origin enable credential phishing and can leak referer context, though the application's own data is not directly read.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can trigger it with a single crafted URL and the redirect target is fully attacker-controlled.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of learning-resource URLs.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, compare req.query.url against a fixed map of permitted destinations and return 400 on a miss.
Alternatively replace the query parameter with a short key that indexes a server-side URL table.

threats.title: Traffic proxied to /profile crosses the trust boundary without security response headers, so injected script runs unrestricted in the session
threats.asset: user profile data rendered on /profile and the victim's authenticated session
threats.attackScenario: Responses returned over the zap-to-app flow from the Express application carry no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or nosniff headers, so an attacker who gets a payload stored in a profile field has it executed when /profile is rendered and uses the victim's logged-in same-origin session to POST to /profile and /memos; the connect.sid cookie itself is HttpOnly, so the script acts as the victim rather than reading the cookie.
assumptions: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
No reverse proxy in front of the Express application injects the missing security headers.
threats.impactReason: Without CSP or framing protection, any injected script acts fully as the victim across profile, memos and allocations pages.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every HTTP response on this flow lacks the headers and the application is reachable by any browser, including the proxied test browser. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-declared helmet middleware on the Express application.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and the helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), frameguard() and hsts() calls in server.js.
Add dont-sniff-mimetype (already in package.json) to set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
Call app.disable("x-powered-by") in server.js.

questions.text: Outside of console.log statements in the error middleware and DAOs, does anything (a logging library, SIEM agent, or log shipper) capture security events like failed logins or benefit/profile changes?
questions.whyAsking: Without durable, searchable security logs, abuse of the benefits or allocations handlers (e.g. tampering with another user's data) could go undetected until real damage is done.
options: No, only console.log output exists, nothing is shipped or retained centrally
Yes, security events are also sent to a log aggregator, file, or monitoring system
Partial - some events are captured but not all sensitive actions
questions.defaultAssumption: Assume no durable security logging exists beyond console.log, so suspicious activity on benefits/allocations handlers is not detectable after the fact.

questions.text: In your actual deployment (not just the docker-compose.yml shown), does the application connect to MongoDB using a username/password for a least-privilege user, rather than an open, credential-less connection?
questions.whyAsking: An unauthenticated MongoDB connection means anyone who can reach the database network (including via an app compromise) has full read/write access to all user, benefit, and financial data.
options: No, the deployed database uses the same credential-less URI as docker-compose.yml
Yes, production uses authenticated, least-privilege database credentials
Unsure how the production database is configured
questions.defaultAssumption: Assume MongoDB authentication is not enabled and the app connects with full, unrestricted access as shown in docker-compose.yml.

questions.text: In production, is HTTPS/TLS terminated somewhere in front of this app (e.g. a load balancer, reverse proxy, or CDN), even though the app itself serves plain HTTP on port 4000?
questions.whyAsking: Without TLS anywhere in the path, session cookies and sensitive data like SSNs and bank account numbers submitted through the benefits/allocations forms would travel in plaintext and could be intercepted.
options: No, traffic is served as plain HTTP with no TLS termination anywhere
Yes, a proxy or load balancer terminates TLS in front of the app
Unsure how production traffic is terminated
questions.defaultAssumption: Assume no TLS termination exists anywhere in the path, so traffic including session cookies and sensitive personal data is transmitted in plaintext.
